Flag processes that list or access environment variables containing secret patterns (API_KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD). Correlate with unexpected child processes from GitHub Actions runners.

suggestion.title: Malicious Code Injection via AI-Generated Commit to Main Branch
suggestion.rationale: Claude Code generates code within GitHub Actions. Article is case study of security risks; no UC detects AI-generated code that deviates from declared intent or contains injected logic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Analyze commits authored by or generated via Claude Code GitHub Actions for anomalies: entropy spikes, obfuscated payloads, system calls outside declared scope, credential-harvesting patterns. Flag commits that introduce network connectivity, file exfiltration, or privilege-escalation logic. Correlate with subsequent build failures or deployment rollbacks.

suggestion.title: Phishing Email from TA4922 Campaign
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'phishing attacks' as the attack vector; this is the primary initial-access mechanism and must be detectable via email gateways and log analysis.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor inbound email for sender addresses, domains, or subject-line patterns consistent with TA4922 phishing campaigns targeting Western nations (UK, Germany, Italy, South Africa). Flag emails with suspicious attachments, authentication requests, or links to credential-harvesting domains.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting Page Access
suggestion.rationale: Multi-region phishing campaigns typically host fake login portals or OAuth consent screens; article target list (UK, Germany, Italy, South Africa) suggests geographically diverse credential collection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect user access to newly registered or spoofed domains impersonating legitimate government, finance, or corporate portals used by targets in the four named regions. Monitor for rapid redirects or form submissions followed by immediate password-reset attempts.

suggestion.title: Malware Payload Execution Post-Phishing Click
suggestion.rationale: After credential theft, phishing campaigns often deliver secondary payloads; article does not exclude malware delivery despite focus on 'phishing,' and TA4922's historical pattern includes post-compromise execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for suspicious process spawns, script execution (PowerShell, VBScript, Cmd), or binary downloads immediately following (1–60 min) email clicks from known phishing senders. Focus on child processes with network connections to suspicious infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Multi-Country Phishing Target Enrichment
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names UK, Germany, Italy, and South Africa as expansion targets; detection use cases must account for region-specific impersonation (e.g., spoofed .uk, .de, .it, .za domains or locale-specific phishing content).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify newly registered or lookalike domains using country-code TLDs (.uk, .de, .it, .za) and homoglyph variants of legitimate government, banking, or corporate entities in the four targeted nations. Cross-reference against phishing-report databases.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Email Attachment Detonation
suggestion.rationale: Phishing campaigns commonly use macro-enabled documents, archives, or executables; article does not exclude attachment-based payloads, and pipeline extracted no file-hash IOCs despite 'phishing' being inherently attachment-prone.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect execution of attachments from phishing emails: .zip files containing .exe, .dll, or macro-enabled Office documents (.docx with enabled content). Monitor for Office child-process spawns (rundll32, regsvr32, PowerShell) within 30 seconds of open.

suggestion.title: TA4922 Command & Control Beaconing
suggestion.rationale: Post-compromise persistence and data exfiltration require C2; article scope (multi-country, likely high-value targets) implies command-and-control infrastructure beyond simple phishing-page redirects.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for outbound connections to known or suspected TA4922 C2 infrastructure (IPs, domains, certificates). Watch for beaconing patterns: regular, low-volume, encrypted HTTPS traffic to non-standard ports or domains from user machines.

suggestion.title: Cisco Unified CM CVE-2026-20230 Exploit Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title states 'Exploit Code Goes Public'—establishes active exploitation risk. No initial-access detection generated despite this being the primary threat vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Cisco Unified CM web interfaces (ports 8443, 8002) for HTTP requests matching CVE-2026-20230 exploit signatures. Alert on POST/GET to vulnerable endpoints, malformed parameters, or request patterns consistent with public PoC code.

suggestion.title: Code Execution via Cisco Unified CM Vulnerability
suggestion.rationale: Public exploit code implies remote code execution capability. Article indicates vulnerability severity; execution-phase detection absent.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect child process spawning from Unified CM services (ccm.exe, tomcat parent) with unexpected process names (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash). Flag unusual parent-child relationships.

suggestion.title: Unusual Admin Account Activity Post Unified CM Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Successful exploitation of VoIP infrastructure typically leads to admin credential abuse or privilege escalation. No privilege-escalation use case generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on new administrative user creation, admin group membership changes, or high-privilege role assignments within Unified CM. Correlate failed logins preceding successful privilege changes.

suggestion.title: External Reconnaissance Targeting Cisco Unified CM
suggestion.rationale: Public exploit availability means attacks originate from external threat actors. Detection should flag anomalous external scanning.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect repeated connection attempts to Unified CM ports (8443, 8002, 7003) from external IPs across short time windows. Flag geographic anomalies in source regions for internal-only service.

suggestion.title: Suspicious HTTP Requests to Cisco WebDialer Service
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted HTTP request to an affected device.' This is the initial delivery vector and should be monitored at the HTTP/application layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor requests to WebDialer endpoints for anomalous patterns: excessive parameter encoding, file:// or unusual protocol schemes in parameters, sizes above baseline, or requests containing path traversal sequences. Flag requests from unexpected source IPs or with high entropy payloads.

suggestion.title: File Write to System Directories from WebDialer Process
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies: 'A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write files to the underlying operating system that could be used later to elevate to root.' Writes to /etc, /root, /bin, cron, or SSH config directories from WebDialer context are the exploitation signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on file writes to privileged system directories (etc, root home, bin, cron directories, SSH config) originating from Cisco Unified CM WebDialer process or its child processes. Correlate temporal proximity with suspicious HTTP activity to WebDialer endpoints.

suggestion.title: Root-Level Process Execution Following WebDialer Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes outcome: 'exploitation of this vulnerability could result in an attacker elevating privileges to root.' Root-level process creation shortly after exploitation attempts indicates successful privilege escalation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag process creation with UID=0 (root) spawned from or in the context of WebDialer service. Look for sudo invocations from WebDialer, new cron jobs with root execution, SSH key installations in /root/.ssh/, or shell spawning from WebDialer child processes.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-20230 PoC Pattern Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'Cisco's PSIRT is aware of publicly available proof-of-concept exploit code for CVE-2026-20230.' PoC payloads may be detected via IDS/WAF signatures or payload analysis once reverse-engineered.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Once PoC payload signatures are identified via threat feeds or reverse engineering, deploy WAF/IDS rules to detect known exploit patterns. Monitor for HTTP requests matching known malicious WebDialer payloads or file-write patterns derived from PoC analysis.

suggestion.title: Cisco Unified CM WebDialer Service Enabled on Non-Telephony Systems
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies: 'WebDialer is disabled by default' and administrations must explicitly enable it. Presence of WebDialer on systems not designated as Unified CM servers or enabling in production after updates suggests attacker persistence or testing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Inventory systems for WebDialer service state and alert when enabled on systems outside approved asset list. Monitor Cisco Unified Serviceability administrative console for unauthorized service activation changes outside scheduled maintenance windows.

suggestion.title: GitHub Action Triggered by Issue Creation
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states 'malicious issue hijack repositories' — attack vector is issue-based workflow trigger. Pipeline failed to identify this execution path.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor GitHub workflow_run and issue events for unexpected trigger chains. Alert on workflows executed by low-privilege accounts or from unfamiliar issue creators. Correlate issue creation timestamp with action execution within <5min window.

suggestion.title: Repository Credential Access via Compromised Action
suggestion.rationale: GitHub Actions hijacking inherently implies access to repository secrets/tokens. Pipeline mentioned no secret exfiltration or credential-access patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag actions that export or print repository secrets, GitHub tokens, or OIDC tokens to logs. Detect unauthorized access to github.token or secrets context. Monitor for base64-encoded credential strings in workflow logs.

suggestion.title: Workflow File Modification via Issue-Triggered Execution
suggestion.rationale: Hijacked action likely modifies .github/workflows to persist access. No detection for unauthorized workflow file changes in pipeline output.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on commits modifying .github/workflows/ or .github/workflows/*.yml from within a GitHub Action context, especially from non-default branches or by bot accounts. Correlate with preceding issue-based triggers.

suggestion.title: OIDC Token Misuse in Actions Context
suggestion.rationale: GitHub Actions OIDC federation is a trust-chain attack surface. No mention of token generation, exfiltration, or cross-org token usage.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for OIDC token exchange (aud=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com) followed by cross-account or cross-org API calls. Detect tokens issued to unexpected principals or used outside normal workflow scope.

suggestion.title: Repository Secret Enumeration in Actions Output
suggestion.rationale: Title mentions hijack but no detection for secret enumeration via action logs or artifact exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on workflows that list or print environment variables, read .env files, or enumerate mounted secrets. Flag artifact uploads containing credential patterns. Monitor action job logs for secrets context access.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement via Compromised GitHub Actions to Downstream Systems
suggestion.rationale: Hijacked action may reach external systems (deployments, cloud infra). Pipeline shows no detection for lateral movement or third-party API calls from action context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on API calls or deployments initiated by GitHub Actions to cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) using compromised tokens. Detect unusual IAM assume-role or deployment credentials used from action context.

suggestion.title: Suspicious GTM Container Loading Malicious JavaScript on Checkout
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'malicious code is embedded in legitimate-looking GTM containers, which activate when a shopper reaches a checkout page'—GTM trust abuse is the initial access vector bypassing CSP filters.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect GTM containers (googletagmanager.com) loading JavaScript that queries Stripe metadata fields or calls new Function() for dynamic code execution. Alert when GTM deployment on checkout pages includes unrecognized tag IDs or containers with recent creation timestamps (article: Dec 24, 2025).

suggestion.title: JavaScript Form-Field Harvesting on Payment Pages
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes capture of 'credit card number, expiration date, CVV code, customer name...billing and email addresses, and phone number'—form enumeration and field access pattern on checkout context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect JavaScript accessing multiple sensitive form field selectors (credit card, CVV, expiration, email, phone) in rapid succession on pages identified as checkout contexts. Alert on patterns of reading .value properties from payment-related input elements.

suggestion.title: XOR-Obfuscated Data Storage in localStorage Before Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'obfuscated using the XOR operation, and stored locally instead of immediately exfiltrated...local file is wiped to eliminate traces'—staging and cleanup pattern indicating deliberate anti-forensics.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect JavaScript storing large hex-encoded or binary-like obfuscated blobs in localStorage with atypical key names (_d_data_customer_ in Firestore variant, or equivalent patterns). Correlate storage writes with preceding form-field access. Alert on subsequent clearing of storage within minutes (anti-forensics).

suggestion.title: Rapid Stripe Customer Object Creation with Stolen Data in Metadata
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Every stolen payment card becomes a fake customer record in the attacker's Stripe account, turning Stripe into a storage backend for stolen data'—abuse of legitimate API endpoint for persistent exfiltration staging.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Stripe API (api.stripe.com) for POST /v1/customers calls with rapid frequency from e-commerce domains. Flag metadata fields containing payment-card-like data, hex strings, or XOR-obfuscated patterns. Alert when customer creation rate exceeds baseline for a merchant account.

suggestion.title: Periodic Automated Exfiltration Routine Triggered on Page Load
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'executes right after a page load and every minute after, by...creating a new Stripe customer object'—recurring scheduled task distinct from one-time data theft.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect JavaScript registering periodic execution handlers (setInterval ≈60 seconds) on page-load events (DOMContentLoaded). Correlate timing with outbound Stripe/Firestore API calls and presence of obfuscated blobs in localStorage. Alert if exfiltration traffic originates from checkout page contexts.

suggestion.title: Firestore Misuse for Malicious Payload Delivery and Data Staging
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Google Firestore...payload is retrieved from a Firestore document named tracking/captcha in a project called braintree-payment-app'—cloud service abuse for C2 and exfil using deceptive project/document naming.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Firestore API queries (firestore.googleapis.com) from frontend JavaScript, especially to projects with payment-service naming (braintree-payment-app) and documents with obfuscated or security-mimicking paths (tracking/captcha). Alert on Firestore reads followed by new Function() calls or localStorage writes.

suggestion.title: Detect 100GB+ Egress Data Transfer to External IPs
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'stolen more than 234 GB of data'—concrete exfiltration threshold for network monitoring.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on cumulative outbound data >100GB/week to non-whitelisted external IPs from servers hosting healthcare databases or file repositories. Correlate with authentication anomalies or privilege escalation events.

suggestion.title: Detect Unauthorized Network Access to Healthcare Systems
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'unauthorized access to a limited portion of our network'—signals initial compromise and internal persistence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for failed authentication bursts followed by successful logins from off-hours or unusual geolocations. Flag VPN/RDP access to sensitive database servers preceding large data queries.

suggestion.title: Detect Bulk PII Collection and Compression
suggestion.rationale: Article: exfiltration of 'email addresses, full names, phone numbers, government-issued IDs, health insurance information, genders, dates of birth'—implies staging and compression of healthcare records.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of archive utilities (7zip, tar, WinRAR) on healthcare database servers or access to PII export tables. Monitor for mass SELECT queries on identity/insurance columns during non-business hours.

suggestion.title: Detect Data Staging to Cloud or External Storage
suggestion.rationale: 234GB dataset suggests intermediate staging before exfiltration—likely cloud bucket uploads, temp shares, or external drive copies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for large file copies to OneDrive, ShareFile, or S3 buckets outside approved backup ranges. Flag creation of temp directories with sizes >10GB. Alert on archive file uploads to external storage services.

suggestion.title: Detect Breach-Forum Registration and Leak-Site Operations
suggestion.rationale: Article: threat actor 'listed the company on its data leak site' after failed extortion—signals threat-intel monitoring of ShinyHunters infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference DNS queries and web proxy logs against known ShinyHunters leak-site domains. Alert if employee credentials or organization artifacts appear in leaked datasets on public threat-intel feeds (HIBP, breach databases).

suggestion.title: Detect Public Healthcare PII Disclosure
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'data was publicly leaked' containing 2.6M records with sensitive healthcare identifiers—critical for breach-response triage and notification triggers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest HIBP and breach-alert feeds for organization name and employee domain mentions. Flag datasets containing >100K records with PII patterns matching your organization's known identity namespace (domain suffixes, employee name patterns).

suggestion.title: Fake Open-Source Tool Repository / Typosquatting Domain Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article headline: 'Fake Sites Mimicking Open-Source Tools Rank High on Google' — core attack vector. Pipeline missed detection for lookalike domain registration and DNS queries to homograph variants of known OSS projects.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on DNS queries and HTTP connections to domains with character substitution (l→1, o→0, rn→m) or similar TLDs targeting well-known OSS names (npm, Python, Go, GitHub projects). Cross-reference domain WHOIS age (< 90 days) with search-engine click-throughs and subsequent file downloads.

suggestion.title: SEO-Poisoned Search Result Click-Through and Download Chain
suggestion.rationale: Title: 'Rank High on Google to Deliver Malware' — establishes search result manipulation as the delivery mechanism. Pipeline did not capture the initial-access pattern of user clicking search results on newly registered domains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP referrer=Google search with destinations to newly-registered or suspicious domains. Alert if referrer includes OSS keywords (npm, pip, git, tool names) and destination performs file download or scripting execution.

suggestion.title: Traffic Direction System (TDS) Redirect Chain Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Deliver Malware via TDS' — describes redirect-based delivery infrastructure. Pipeline did not identify TDS-specific patterns (multiple fast 302/307 redirects, domain-hopping, or IP-based intermediate redirects).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP redirect chains with ≥2 hops to different domains within <2 seconds, especially when originated from fake tool repositories. Flag redirects to known TDS providers or IP-based intermediate redirects. Monitor for final payload delivery to malware-hosting domains.

suggestion.title: Executable Download and Immediate Execution from Fake Repository
suggestion.rationale: Attack flow requires file download from fake site (claiming to be OSS tool) and execution. Pipeline missed the execution-chain detection linking download source to process creation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect executable or archive downloads from lookalike domains followed by extraction and execution within 5 minutes. Alert on process creation with parent = explorer.exe or cmd.exe and file origin from unusual domain or temporary directory.

suggestion.title: Malware C2 Beaconing Post-TDS Delivery
suggestion.rationale: Article describes malware delivery endpoint; post-infection C2 communication should be detected. Pipeline did not establish detection for callback traffic from executed payloads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for DNS queries and HTTP connections from processes spawned by executables downloaded from fake OSS domains. Alert on irregular intervals, small payloads, or communications to infrastructure previously associated with TDS or malware-as-a-service platforms.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Installer Execution Post-Ad Network Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'spreads via malicious Google and YouTube Ads'—establishes initial access pathway (user clicks ad → downloads → executes). Pipeline generated no use case for installer/DMG execution following ad platform beaconing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for DMG or .app execution originating from ~/Downloads or /tmp within 2 minutes of ad-network traffic (google.com, gstatic.com, youtube.com referrers). Flag process chains: browser → curl/wget → installer execution, especially unsigned binaries.

suggestion.title: macOS Backdoor Persistence via Launch Agent or Dylib Loading
suggestion.rationale: FlutterShell is identified as a backdoor, implying persistence mechanism post-initial-access. Article provides no detail but use case is foundational for backdoor detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect creation of LaunchAgent plist files in ~/Library/LaunchAgents or dylib injection by processes matching installers/ads. Correlate with unsigned code signatures or recent file modifications to system-adjacent paths.

suggestion.title: Command and Control Beaconing (Backdoor C2)
suggestion.rationale: Backdoor-class malware necessarily performs C2 callbacks. Pipeline failed to surface network-based detection for backdoor phone-home behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound connections from suspicious macOS processes to non-standard ports (not 80/443/53) or to recently-registered domains. Baseline expected traffic from installer processes post-execution; flag anomalous callback patterns or encrypted tunnels.

suggestion.title: Ad-Served Malware Click-to-Download Timeline Correlation
suggestion.rationale: Core attack vector stated as 'malicious Google and YouTube Ads'—requires detection linking user ad exposure/click, network traffic to ad platforms, and subsequent file write to Downloads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate browser referrer headers from ad platforms (google.com, gstatic.com) with file write events in ~/Downloads within 30 seconds, followed by file execute events. Flag where referrer domain does not match expected benign ad network traffic patterns.

suggestion.title: Stata process spawning Python with shell metacharacters in command context
suggestion.rationale: Article states attacker can inject 'python' commands via log_file_name. Should hunt for Stata spawning python.exe/python directly, specifically in response to log_file_name parameter with shell syntax (quotes, semicolons, backslash-n)—distinguishes exploitation from legitimate Python data processing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate: Stata process execution with command line containing 'log_file_name' and shell metacharacters (backslash-n, quotes) within same invocation, immediately followed by child process creation (python, sh, cmd). Tight timing window (< 5 seconds) and command-line correlation reduces FP.

suggestion.title: MCP-for-Stata API call with newline-escaped log_file_name parameter
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'quotes, newline' as injection vectors into log_file_name. Should hunt for API/CLI logs showing log_file_name parameters containing literal or escaped newlines (\n, %0a) which break statement boundaries in Stata.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt MCP-for-Stata API request logs for stata_do() or similar calls where log_file_name parameter contains newline encoding (\n, %0a, \r\n) or quote escaping attempts. These patterns directly exploit the 'unsan­itized interpolation' described in article.

suggestion.title: Stata erase command execution via log_file_name injection
suggestion.rationale: Article names 'erase' (file deletion) as example injected command. Should hunt for Stata erase builtin preceded by suspicious log_file_name invocation—indicates file destruction post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Log file containing 'erase' command or file deletion events correlated with preceding Stata invocation where log_file_name parameter contains shell syntax. Article's 'GuardValidator bypassed' control means no safe-guard on the parameter itself.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Mail Folder Rules on Executive Mailbox
suggestion.rationale: Five-month mailbox surveillance requires persistence mechanism; article premise implies attacker maintained access via folder rules, forwarding rules, or delegate permissions to exfiltrate emails without user detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on creation or modification of mail forwarding rules, folder rules, or mailbox delegates on executive or high-value accounts, especially rules that move or copy mail to external domains or forwarding to uncommon addresses.

suggestion.title: Anomalous OAuth App Consent Grants on Executive Mailbox
suggestion.rationale: Modern email compromise often uses OAuth app permissions rather than password theft; attacker would need to grant consent to exfiltration application, appearing as T1528 (unauthorized credentials).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unusual OAuth app consent events for Microsoft Graph mail.read permissions on high-value accounts, especially from non-corporate IP ranges, unusual geolocations, or during off-hours.

suggestion.title: Bulk Mail Access and Exfiltration Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article states espionage over 5 months; attacker must have accessed and exfiltrated large volumes of emails. This is collection phase (T1114) followed by exfiltration (T1020).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on ExecuteSearch or bulk folder reads followed by unusual outbound SMTP/IMAP traffic or attachment downloads to non-corporate cloud services; baseline normal mailbox access and alert on deviations >3σ in volume over 5-month window.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement from Compromised Executive Account
suggestion.rationale: Email compromise of executive is typically pivot point for broader network compromise; attacker would likely enumerate other accounts, grant permissions, or launch phishing from this trusted account.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate anomalous login activity from compromised mailbox account (cross-tenant logins, impossible travel) with subsequent privilege escalation or mailbox creation attempts; flag if compromised account is used for phishing campaign template generation.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Inbox Filtering and Retention Manipulation
suggestion.rationale: Attacker must hide evidence of mailbox access; would likely create rules to suppress notifications, delete audit logs, or move sensitive emails to hidden folders to avoid detection during 5-month window.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on mailbox audit log deletion, rule creation to suppress read/access notifications, or inbox folder hiding on executive accounts; baseline expected audit log size and alert if logs are suspiciously truncated or show gaps.

suggestion.title: Multi-Tenancy or Federated Trust Abuse in Email Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'stock exchange executive' without specifying single-tenant environment; modern sophisticated attacks on financial institutions exploit federated trusts, cross-tenant access, or B2B partner connections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual consent grants or sign-in events from federated partner tenants or multi-tenant applications; alert if executive account is accessed from tenant-external OAuth app or cross-tenant resource sharing policies are relaxed.

suggestion.title: PowerShell Encoded Command Execution from cmd.exe Spawn
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes: 'cmd.exe process spawning powershell.exe with an -EncodedCommand parameter containing a Base64-encoded payload.' Canonical living-off-the-land execution pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor cmd.exe spawning powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand, -enc, or -e flags. Decode Base64 command-line arguments and inspect for invoke-expression, System.Net, DownloadFile, or HTTP fetch keywords. Cross-correlate process parent/child with outbound network connections on non-standard ports.

suggestion.title: Invoke-WebRequest Download to User AppData Folder
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'Invoke-WebRequest to fetch a file named script.ps1, dropping it into the user's ApplicationData directory.' File downloads to user temp folders are high-risk ingress indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on Invoke-WebRequest or DownloadFile method calls in PowerShell context where destination is %APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, or %TEMP%. Flag .ps1 file creation in these locations. Correlate with parent process being powershell.exe spawned from cmd.exe or other unusual parent.

suggestion.title: Anti-Forensics via Remove-Item File Deletion
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'Remove-Item, attempting to delete traces of the downloaded script.' Deletion of recently-written files via Remove-Item is direct defense-evasion evidence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag Remove-Item or del commands targeting recently-created files (within 10 minutes) in user writable directories. Correlate with preceding Invoke-WebRequest or encoded PowerShell execution. High fidelity if Remove-Item parent is powershell.exe spawned from suspicious ancestor.

suggestion.title: Outbound C2 Confirmed by Firewall IP + EDR Process Correlation
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes multi-domain correlation: 'firewall and endpoint data in a way that neither source could have accomplished alone'—firewall shows 144.31.221.82 connection, EDR confirms curl.exe and powershell.exe processes at same timestamp initiating those connections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt: Identify outbound connections to known-bad IPs or ASNs (via threat feeds, historical C2, or reputation scoring). Cross-check EDR for process execution (curl, powershell, wget, msiexec, python) matching connection timestamp ±5 seconds. Confirm if process parent is unusual (cmd.exe, explorer.exe, winword.exe, svchost.exe).

suggestion.title: Traffic Direction System (TDS) Redirect Pattern Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article describes initial compromise: 'compromised website redirects visitors through a chain of intermediate servers before landing on a malicious payload host'—specifically 144.31.221.82 port 6060 path /capcha9856.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect connections to known TDS infrastructure (144.31.221.82:6060, /capcha* paths). Look for redirect chains: user initiates HTTP request to legitimate-looking domain, receives redirect to intermediate IPs before final payload delivery. Flag unusual User-Agent strings matching attacker infrastructure IPs.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Tool Execution: curl/MSIEXEC/Python from Workstations at Off-Hours
suggestion.rationale: Article hunt hypothesis: 'A curl binary running on a finance team's workstation at 2am is not the same signal as curl running in a CI/CD pipeline.' Baseline deviations in tool usage are hunting indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline normal tool usage (curl, python, wget, msiexec, powershell) by user role and time-of-day. Flag anomalous execution: curl on finance workstation outside business hours, python on non-dev system downloading from internet, msiexec fetching remote payloads. Correlate with destination reputation (malicious ASN, known C2 range).

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm post-install script spawning unexpected processes
suggestion.rationale: Title states 'Self-Spreading Worm'—worm propagation in npm supply chain occurs via post-install lifecycle scripts that execute arbitrary code, typically spawning shells or invoking other package managers. This is the primary execution vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm.exe or node.exe spawning PowerShell, cmd, bash, or python children with arguments suggesting file exfiltration, network beaconing, or recursive npm install commands. Flag post-install context (parent process contains 'install' or 'postinstall' script reference).

suggestion.title: Native module compilation with obfuscated or remote gyp scripts
suggestion.rationale: Attack explicitly leverages 'binding.gyp'—node-gyp's native build config file. Malicious gyp scripts can execute arbitrary C/C++ code or shell commands during npm install. Detection must catch gyp invocation with suspicious inline or downloaded scripts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on gyp.exe or python.exe execution initiated by npm with command-line references to binding.gyp files; correlate with child processes spawning cmd/powershell/curl. Flag gyp execution where binding.gyp was downloaded or modified post-install.

suggestion.title: Recursive or cascading npm package installations from single command
suggestion.rationale: 'Self-Spreading Worm' indicates malicious package triggers installation of other malicious packages, creating dependency-chain propagation. Detection should identify abnormal install cascades where one install spawns many child installs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm install command spawning 3+ child npm processes within 2 minutes, each installing different packages, where packages are not declared in package.json. Correlate with post-install script execution timing.

suggestion.title: npm process network communication during installation phase
suggestion.rationale: Worms typically beacon to attacker infrastructure to confirm infection and coordinate propagation. npm processes should only contact official registries during normal operation; unexpected outbound connections indicate data exfiltration or command retrieval.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block and alert on npm.exe or node.exe establishing outbound TCP/UDP connections to non-standard domains or high-numbered ports outside registry.npmjs.org, registry.yarnpkg.com, and official CDNs. Trigger especially if connection occurs during postinstall script phase.

suggestion.title: System persistence mechanisms planted by npm post-install scripts
suggestion.rationale: Self-spreading worms establish persistence to survive process termination and re-execute. npm post-install scripts can invoke native code to create scheduled tasks, registry Run keys, or cron jobs. Detection must catch these system-level modifications.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm child processes (or their descendants) modifying HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, creating scheduled tasks via schtasks.exe, or modifying cron/systemd. Alert on any registry write or task creation originating from npm post-install context.

suggestion.title: npm preinstall hook binary execution
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'Rust ELF binary executed via preinstall' and 'pushing malicious commits into repositories.' This is the core execution mechanism yet no detection exists.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process execution spawned by npm package lifecycle hooks (preinstall, postinstall, prepare). Flag Rust/ELF binaries executed from ~/.npm or node_modules with unusual command-line arguments or network connectivity.

suggestion.title: npm account compromise with package republish
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'asteroiddao account...published package versions' and 'can publish trojanized versions of packages owned by the victim.' Detects initial compromise-to-abuse chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect new package versions published from known-trusted developer accounts with: (1) divergent content hash from baseline, (2) new binary payloads, (3) new preinstall scripts, or (4) auth origin geochange + first-publish in 90+ days.

suggestion.title: git commit timestamp anomaly (timestamp spoofing)
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'commit timestamps point to several years ago, up to 13 years...though they were pushed in the past few days. This is likely to evade investigation.' Clear evasion indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag git commits where authored-date is >180 days older than commit-date, especially in security-sensitive repositories or during package version updates. Cross-correlate with rare publisher activity.

suggestion.title: mass environment variable and credential file enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'targets 86 environment variables (key-value pairs) and 20 credential files...OpenAI, AWS, Anthropic...SSH keys, Exodus cryptocurrency wallet files.' Detects credential access phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect processes accessing or enumerating known credential paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.vault, ~/.config) and environment variable dumps (e.g., env, printenv) in non-interactive or CI contexts. Correlate with package installation or build steps.

suggestion.title: GitHub Actions artifact exfiltration of secrets
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'serializes the secrets into a single value and then writes it to a file with a harmless-looking name, as if it were lint or formatting output. The last step of the process is uploading the file as a build artifact.' Describes data exfil via CI.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor GitHub Actions workflow artifacts for files containing serialized environment variable data, base64-encoded credential material, or JSON blobs with API keys. Flag artifact uploads from unfamiliar workflows or outside-hours CI runs.

suggestion.title: Tor network connections from development/CI environments
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'communicates with the operator over the Tor network.' Detects C2 callback and data exfil transport.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on outbound Tor entry-node connections (port 6667, 9001, 9030) or Tor HTTPS bridges from non-VPN developer machines and CI runners. Correlate with npm/git activity or package build invocations.

suggestion.title: Suspicious App Installation via Masqueraded Utility Apps
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware delivered via 'Fake News, PDF and War Map Apps' — explicit social engineering infection vector with fake app masquerading. Pipeline failed to suggest detection for initial access via deceptive app naming/branding.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for installation of apps with innocuous names (news readers, PDF viewers, maps) from non-Play Store sources or newly registered publishers. Correlate with regional targeting indicators (Arabic language, Middle East region targeting).

suggestion.title: Spyware Permission Abuse — Microphone/Camera/Contact Access
suggestion.rationale: Article characterizes tool as 'spyware' with implicit data collection mandate, but pipeline missed detection for dangerous permission combinations (audio/video/contact capture) typical of surveillance malware.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on apps with suspicious permissions (RECORD_AUDIO, CAMERA, READ_CONTACTS, READ_CALL_LOG, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, READ_SMS) granted to masqueraded utility apps. Correlate permission abuse with communication events and data access logs.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration via Unauthorized Network Communications
suggestion.rationale: Spyware's defining characteristic is stealing user data (contacts, location, messages, calls). No detection use case generated for exfiltration phase despite this being core attack objective.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline for app network behavior. Alert on encrypted traffic to non-standard ports, traffic to newly registered domains, or bulk data transfers from installed APKs matching Asin family indicators.

suggestion.title: Defense Evasion via App Code Obfuscation and Hidden Receivers
suggestion.rationale: Malware targeting geopolitically sensitive region (Arabic users, war-themed lure) suggests sophistication and likely anti-analysis techniques. Pipeline did not suggest evasion detection patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Analyze APK manifests for obfuscated strings, dynamic code loading (reflection, ClassLoader calls), hidden broadcast receivers, and suspicious runtime permissions. Cross-reference with APK scanning tools (VirusTotal, Koodous).

suggestion.title: Command & Control Communication Detection for Mobile Malware
suggestion.rationale: Spyware requires C2 channel for commanding exfiltration and receiving updates. Article does not expose C2 indicators but pipeline should flag this gap and suggest C2 detection baseline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS requests and network flows from newly installed apps for connection to known malware C2 infrastructure. Build detection based on confirmed Asin family C2 indicators once article is fully parsed; alert on similar patterns from other masqueraded apps.

suggestion.title: Brickstorm WebSocket C2 Communications Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies malware 'uses the WebSocket protocol for C2 communications and a multiplexing library for simultaneous data streams to the server.' Deployed across Egnyte, pfSense, Linux servers over 18+ months undetected.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for persistent WebSocket connections from non-standard sources (edge appliances, NAS, storage sync systems). Alert on multiplexed simultaneous streams from single process. Profile normal Egnyte/NAS egress first to establish baseline.

suggestion.title: Plenet .NET Backdoor Execution on Synology NAS
suggestion.rationale: Plenet 'also tracked as Grimbolt by Google, is a cross-platform .NET-based backdoor' deployed to Synology NAS appliance for 'interactive shell access, remote command execution, file manipulation, and command-and-control server switching.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for .NET runtime or .NET assemblies executing on Synology NAS (atypical for firmware baseline). Look for dynamic C2 server switching: single malware process changing destination IPs/domains mid-session.

suggestion.title: SSL VPN Abuse to Evade M365 Conditional Access
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'accessed the organization's Microsoft 365 enevironment' via 'Brickstorm proxying features and stolen credentials' specifically 'to blend in with legitimate network traffic and evade Conditional Access policies that would have otherwise prevented access.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate M365 logins originating from SSL VPN with Brickstorm proxy infrastructure. Flag successful M365 logins from SSL VPN that bypass or predate Conditional Access log entries. Monitor for Brickstorm's WebSocket multiplexing behavior on VPN gateway egress.

suggestion.title: MSP Infrastructure Pivot to Customer Network
suggestion.rationale: Article describes MSP compromise where 'Volexity found that VerdantBamboo had planted a BSD variant of Brickstorm on a pfSense firewall.' Later: 'The researchers have medium confidence that the attacker pivoted from the MSP into the victim organization's environment.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for internal network access originating from customer-managed MSP edge devices (pfSense, SD-WAN appliances) to customer-owned resources with unusual timing or destinations. Flag cross-customer lateral flows from shared MSP infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Egnyte Storage Sync System Compromise and C2 Beaconing
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'VerdantBamboo compromised an Egnyte Storage Sync system and accessed it periodically through the victim's web SSL VPN,' establishing persistent foothold for 18+ months before detection and initial attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Egnyte Storage Sync logs for unexpected process spawning or lateral code execution attempts. Baseline normal Egnyte network peers and alert on connections to infrastructure tied to Brickstorm (Golang/Rust binaries, WebSocket destinations). Hunt for periodic outbound connections (periodic access pattern) inconsistent with backup behavior.

suggestion.title: AgentPSD Python Reverse Shell Fallback Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'AgentPSD is a simple Python-based reverse shell utility that Volexity believes VerdantBamboo used as a fallback persistence mechanism.' Configured to connect to different C2 domain than primary Brickstorm implant, indicating intentional multi-stage persistence design.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for suspicious Python processes on edge systems (Synology NAS, pfSense, retired Linux email archive). Look for Python executing socket code to C2 domain distinct from primary malware infrastructure. Use YARA rules for Python reverse shell markers (socket.socket, subprocess.Popen patterns).

suggestion.title: BRICKSTORM Malware Execution on Network Appliances
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly identifies 'custom malware toolkit' (BRICKSTORM) targeting 'firewalls, storage systems, and network appliances.' No execution-phase detection generated despite 12 malware hashes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for process/binary execution on firewalls and appliances matching BRICKSTORM hash signatures. Alert on spawning of child processes, network callbacks, or file modifications inconsistent with normal appliance operation.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated Malware on Network Devices (T1027)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly maps T1027 (Obfuscation) and describes malware 'without ever tripping an alarm' for 'well over a year,' indicating sophisticated code obfuscation. No defense-evasion detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect obfuscated/packed binaries on appliances via entropy analysis, abnormal PE headers, or missing legitimate vendor signatures. Baseline clean appliance firmware and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: Long-Dwell Persistence via Appliance Admin Account Manipulation
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'quietly living inside corporate networks for well over a year' explicitly indicates long-term persistence. No persistence-phase UC generated despite implicit account/credential compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor appliance admin login activity for anomalies: off-hours access, repeated failed logins preceding success, bulk configuration changes, new service accounts, or credential resets. Baseline normal admin behavior and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: Exploitation of Appliance Management Interfaces
suggestion.rationale: Compromise of management-restricted devices (firewalls, storage) requires initial access through exploitation or trusted channels. Article implies multi-appliance compromise. No initial-access UC generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for exploitation attempts against appliance web interfaces and SSH/Telnet: command injection, SQL injection, XXE payloads, path traversal in HTTP traffic to management ports (443, 8443, 22, 23). Alert on successful admin logins from unexpected IPs/ASNs outside maintenance windows.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Configuration Persistence on Firewalls and Storage
suggestion.rationale: Multi-year dwell time requires maintenance of backdoor/access mechanism. Article describes 'custom malware toolkit' suggesting installed persistence hooks. No persistence-mechanism UC generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on appliance configuration changes outside change windows: modifications to admin credentials, authentication policies, scheduled tasks, startup configurations, or SAML/OAuth settings. Review bulk config changes during non-business hours.

suggestion.title: Command-and-Control Beaconing from Network Appliances
suggestion.rationale: Continuous presence for '12+ months' requires active C2 for malware command/control and data exfiltration. Article provides no mention of detected C2 activity, implying sophisticated evasion. No C2-phase UC generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline normal outbound communication from firewalls (syslog, NTP, DNS, firmware updates). Alert on anomalous destinations (rare IPs, non-CDN), protocols unusual for device type (DNS tunneling, HTTP exfil), periodic beaconing, or high-volume data transfers inconsistent with appliance role.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U CVE-2026-28318 DoS via deflate POST
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'specially crafted POST requests that crash the Serv-U service without authentication using Content-Encoding: deflate'. This is a direct attack signature that should trigger detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect POST requests to Serv-U endpoints (default ports 43, 43/TCP) containing Content-Encoding: deflate header. Alert on clusters of such requests within short timeframes, indicating DoS probe or attack. Filter out legitimate client POST operations where possible.

suggestion.title: Serv-U pre-15.5.4 version detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states SolarWinds released 15.5.4 Hotfix 1 as patch. Organizations can be scanned for unpatched versions prior to 15.5.4, enabling rapid asset targeting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify Serv-U instances reporting version < 15.5.4 via banner grab, version endpoint, or service enumeration. Flag these as vulnerable to CVE-2026-28318 and prioritize for patching alerts. Correlate with external Shodan/Censys scans to validate exposure.

suggestion.title: Serv-U service crash or restart events
suggestion.rationale: Article describes the vulnerability as causing service crashes. Sudden, repeated restarts or abnormal terminations of Serv-U process may indicate active exploitation attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Serv-U process termination and rapid restart cycles (>3 restarts in 10 minutes). Correlate with network POST traffic from external IPs to confirm DoS attack pattern. High false-positive risk if service is legitimately restarted for patching.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Deflate-Encoded POST Exploit Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'specially crafted POST requests using the Content-Encoding: deflate header' as the attack vector. This is a direct behavioral signature and the most specific IOC in the article.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for POST requests to Serv-U services (ports 22, 3389, or application-specific) with Content-Encoding: deflate header. This header is abnormal in production traffic and serves as the trigger for the vulnerability. Alert on any hits, baseline false positives by source.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Service Crash or Abnormal Restart
suggestion.rationale: Article states the exploit 'crash[es] the Serv-U service without authentication.' Service termination events are detectable via process logs, Windows Event Log, or monitoring agents.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected Serv-U process termination (Event ID 4689 on Windows, process exit signals on Linux). Correlate timing with inbound POST requests. Establish baseline restart frequency and flag anomalies, especially if no scheduled maintenance occurred.

suggestion.title: Unpatched CVE-2026-28318 in Asset Inventory
suggestion.rationale: Article names CVE-2026-28318 explicitly with federal remediation deadline 2026-06-19. Vulnerability scanners must flag unpatched Serv-U instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query vulnerability management platform for Serv-U instances with CVE-2026-28318 status. Filter for unpatched, defer-patched, or unscanned hosts. Cross-reference against network-facing asset inventory. Prioritize remediation by federal due date to avoid compliance findings.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Public-Facing Exposure Hunt
suggestion.rationale: Article references T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application), implying Serv-U instances accessible from the internet. Exposed instances are prime exploitation targets.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Enumerate all Serv-U instances across the network and verify exposure scope. Check firewall rules, network segmentation, and DMZ placement. Flag any instances reachable from external networks on standard Serv-U ports. Correlate with patch status and prioritize exposure reduction.

suggestion.title: Phishing Domain Access — FIFA 2026 Typosquatting
suggestion.rationale: Article opens with 'Fake Sites'—establishes phishing infrastructure as attack entry point. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs or kill-chain phases despite explicit reference.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains matching FIFA event typosquatting patterns (edit-distance < 3 from fifa.com, world-cup.net, etc.) or domains registered within 6 months of tournament. Cross-reference with known phishing blocklists and passive DNS.

suggestion.title: Banking Malware Execution — Suspicious PE from Archive
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names 'Banking Malware' as active payload. Pipeline identified zero execution-phase techniques or behavioral indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect extraction of PE executables from ZIP/RAR archives downloaded from non-corporate sources, followed by immediate execution from temp/user paths. Alert on process trees where explorer.exe or WinRAR spawn rundll32.exe or direct exe execution within 5 seconds of extraction.

suggestion.title: Credential Submission to Attacker-Controlled Hosts
suggestion.rationale: Article lists 'Stolen Logins' as outcome. No credential_access phase or harvest detection was suggested despite this being the stated damage.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for POST requests to non-whitelisted domains carrying credential-like payloads (email+password form submissions, OAuth tokens in query strings). Cross-reference destination IPs against known phishing/C2 OSINT feeds. Alert if user submits credentials to URL flagged as suspicious by hostname reputation or WHOIS age.

suggestion.title: Banking Malware C2 Beaconing — HTTPS Anomaly
suggestion.rationale: Banking malware requires command infrastructure; article implies active campaigns ('already live'). No command_and_control phase was modeled.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify HTTPS traffic to low-reputation or newly-registered C2 domains from banking software processes (winlogon.exe, lsass.exe, svchost.exe child processes). Flag encrypted traffic to non-standard ports (8443, 8888, 9090) or domains with entropy > 4.5. Correlate with process hollowing or DLL injection patterns.

suggestion.title: MFA Bypass or Session Hijacking — Phished Login Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline failed to model exfiltration or abuse of 'Stolen Logins'—the stated end-game. Accounts with compromised credentials are used post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on successful logins immediately following phishing activity, especially from IP/location not previously associated with user. Monitor for rapid-succession account access from multiple FIFA-phishing-linked IPs or devices. Flag impossible-travel scenarios (e.g., login from phishing location + internal network within 15 min).

suggestion.title: Malware Payload Delivery via Email Attachment — FIFA Campaign
suggestion.rationale: Article title specifies malware distribution. Pipeline did not extract attachment IOCs, file hashes, or email-based delivery mechanics despite 'phishing + malware' being core attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for email messages with subjects matching FIFA World Cup keywords (ticket, registration, draw, bracket, etc.) bearing executable or macro-enabled Office attachments. Block or quarantine ZIP/RAR containing PE executables. Flag emails originating from free email providers or spoofed FIFA domain variants.

suggestion.title: DbGate unauthenticated login endpoint (T1078.001 bypass)
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'none auth provider issues JWT tokens without credentials via POST /auth/login'—this is the zero-friction entry point. Pipeline missed the initial-access detection entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on POST /auth/login with HTTP 200 response when request body is empty, null, or missing username/password fields. Correlate timing with subsequent /api/archive/unzip from same source within 60 seconds. High fidelity if preceded by network reconnaissance (GET /auth/login probe).

suggestion.title: ZIP extraction with embedded path traversal (T1190 exploitation)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'malicious ZIP with ../ entries'—the unzip function is the exploitation vector. No detection suggested for the actual malicious file signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for POST to /api/archive/unzip endpoints; correlate with FileCreated events where parent process is node and file_path matches string pattern '*/*/../*'. Alert if extracted file lands outside intended directory tree (e.g., extraction to /app/archive but file appears in /etc).

suggestion.title: Root-context persistence: cron job injection from web process (T1053.003)
suggestion.rationale: Article implies cron-based persistence post-exploitation; T1053.003 is MITRE-mapped but no specific hunt for the write signal. Phrase: 'writes files anywhere on filesystem... runs as root'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on FileCreated/FileModified where InitiatingProcessFileName == 'node' AND InitiatingProcessUser == 'root' AND (FolderPath == '/etc/cron.d' OR FolderPath == '/var/spool/cron' OR FolderPath startswith '/etc/cron.'). Correlate with unzip operation within 30 seconds. Validate file permissions and content for shell invocations.

suggestion.title: Web shell persistence (T1505.003 Server Software Component)
suggestion.rationale: Article lists T1505.003 as a technique but no hunt targets it. Attacker achieves RCE as root; web shell placement in public directory is obvious next step.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on FileCreated where InitiatingProcessFileName == 'node' AND file_extension in (.php, .jsp, .js, .py, .sh) AND FolderPath contains web-root patterns (/var/www, /srv/http, /app/public, /home/*/public_html). Add secondary trigger if file is subsequently executed or network connection initiated from same process.

suggestion.title: Root-owned reverse shell post-exploitation (T1059.004 Unix Shell)
suggestion.rationale: Attack culminates in code execution as root: 'DbGate runs as root in Docker'. No detection for outbound callbacks or interactive shell spawning from compromised process.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child process creation (sh, bash, nc, perl, python, ruby) spawned by node process with InitiatingProcessUser == 'root'. Correlate with unexpected outbound network connections (DeviceNetworkEvents) from root-owned process to non-RFC1918 IP on high ports. Alert on stdin/stdout redirection patterns in command-line arguments.

suggestion.title: Filesystem writes by ait-bsc to paths outside baseline log directory
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'arbitrary file append' and 'bypass the configured log root'—yet no UC directly hunts for file-creation anomalies. UC_1_1 uses researcher-specific paths. Should detect any Filesystem.action=created/modified by ait-bsc process where path != /var/opt/ait-bsc/logs*.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: The compromised BSC process writes files to unexpected locations (detected via unexpected WRITE_FILE events outside its baselin directory). Correlate InitiatingProcessName=ait-bsc or python* with HTTP listener context.

suggestion.title: HTTP POST with path-traversal payload to /*/start endpoint — network baseline absent
suggestion.rationale: UC_1_2 exists but targets internal logs. Article notes 'over the network by unauthenticated attacker'—need to surface when this HTTP API is exposed to untrusted networks (not just local). Network-layer detection of POST with traversal payloads from external/untrusted subnets.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Inbound HTTP POST to a server known to run ait-bsc, targeting path pattern */start, with query/body containing path traversal indicators and originating from an IP not in baseline (non-VPN, non-corporate, non-NASA networks).

suggestion.title: Log files or config files modified by unauthenticated HTTP request (content-injection hypothesis)
suggestion.rationale: T1659 (Content Injection) is listed but no hunt for it. If attacker appends to log files or config, downstream processing may be poisoned. Article explicitly states 'arbitrary file append'—need detection for suspicious mutations of well-known files (syslog, cron, sudoers, httpd.conf, etc.).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: BSC or HTTP daemon writes to critical system files (/etc/*, /var/log/*, /var/spool/cron/*) where write-source is the HTTP listener or its subprocess, and write content does not match known legitimate operations.

suggestion.title: Detect Unauthenticated Requests to Everest Forms Plugin Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Title: 'Hackers Exploit Critical Everest Forms Pro WordPress Plugin Flaw'—core attack is unauthenticated access to vulnerable plugin endpoints; must detect POST/GET payloads to /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP requests to /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/ endpoints with POST method from non-admin source IPs, especially with base64/URL-encoded payloads, serialized PHP objects, or SQL metacharacters in query parameters. Establish baseline of legitimate plugin requests to exclude admin configuration URLs.

suggestion.title: Detect Admin User Creation Post-Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'site takeover'—exploitation payload creates rogue admin via WordPress user/role API or direct database insert, detectable via wp-json/wp/v2/users endpoint or wp_usermeta database writes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unauthenticated POST requests to WordPress REST API /wp-json/wp/v2/users with role='administrator' or capability grants. Correlate with successful exploitation traffic to plugin endpoints within 1-5 minute window. Alert if admin user created with generic/suspicious names (admin2, test, backup, etc.).

suggestion.title: Detect PHP File Creation in Everest Forms Plugin Directory
suggestion.rationale: Successful exploitation typically leaves backdoor or webshell in /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/; file integrity violation combined with HTTP timing provides forensic signal.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag creation or modification of .php files in /wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/ by apache/www-data process with file timestamp within 10 seconds of HTTP POST to plugin endpoint returning 200/201. Exclude expected updates from legitimate plugin auto-updates by version checking.

suggestion.title: Detect RCE via Web Server Process Execution of Suspicious Commands
suggestion.rationale: Unauthenticated RCE via plugin flaw results in code execution as web server user (apache/php-fpm); detect spawning of system commands from php.exe/apache parent.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation by php.exe, apache2, or nginx with parent process coming from web server with command-line containing base64 decoding, PowerShell invocation, curl/wget, or bash -c. Baseline legitimate PHP process spawning (ImageMagick, ffmpeg) and exclude; flag anomalous execution timing correlating with HTTP requests to Everest Forms endpoints.

suggestion.title: Detect Privilege Escalation via WordPress Capability Modification
suggestion.rationale: Post-exploitation persistence requires elevating injected user to admin; detectable via SQL updates to wp_usermeta or wp_options tables granting editor/admin caps to previously low-privilege user.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for UPDATE queries to wp_usermeta WHERE meta_key LIKE '%capabilities%' with role=administrator or wp_options table updates to user_roles. Alert if performed by mysql user running as SYSTEM (compromised web server context) or from connection originating outside normal admin CIDR. Cross-reference with user creation in same time window.

suggestion.title: Detect Suspicious Configuration Changes to Everest Forms Settings
suggestion.rationale: Attackers may modify plugin settings (webhook URLs, email handlers, form handlers) to establish C2 or exfiltration channel; detectable via wp_options or direct serialized option updates.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor wp-admin/admin.php?page=everest-forms* requests for OPTIONS/POST modifying plugin settings, especially email, webhook, or callback URLs. Flag changes pointing to external IPs, non-standard ports, or domains not matching site principal domain. Baseline legitimate configuration changes by site admins; alert on changes from non-admin IP sources.

suggestion.title: npm Package Post-Install Script Code Execution
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks via npm leverage malicious post-install scripts to execute arbitrary code during package installation. Title confirms 'npm in Supply Chain Attacks' but no detection for script-based execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for PowerShell, cmd.exe, or node.exe spawned during npm install phases with file I/O to registry hives, credential stores, or exfiltration endpoints. Flag unexpected network connections initiated by npm-spawned child processes to non-standard registries or external C2 infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Anomalous npm Package Dependency Chain
suggestion.rationale: Malware variants like 'Miasma Worm' in supply chain attacks often use dependency confusion or typosquatting to inject malicious transitives. No use case detected for abnormal transitive dependency resolution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on package.json changes that introduce dependencies with names similar to popular packages (off by one character, different scope), or packages published to npm registry shortly before first installation by rare downstream consumers. Cross-reference package provenance against package-lock.json hash mismatches.

suggestion.title: IronWorm / Miasma Malware Artifact Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article titles two specific malware families (IronWorm, Miasma Worm Variant) but pipeline extracted zero IOCs—no hash signatures, behavioral patterns, or file paths associated with these families.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create signatures for known file paths, registry keys, and mutexes associated with IronWorm and Miasma Worm variants. Monitor for process creation with known command-line patterns or environment variable injection used by these malware families (e.g., IRONWORM_ID, MIASMA_STAGE2).

suggestion.title: npm Registry Authentication Bypass or Credential Theft
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks on npm often steal developer credentials or use .npmrc tokens to publish malicious versions. No detection surfaced for credential access or authentication abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on reads of .npmrc files, .npm-cli-login tokens, or npm cache directories by non-npm processes. Flag unexpected npm publish commands from low-entropy or newly-compromised developer accounts, especially when targeting packages with high install volume.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Package Metadata Spoofing
suggestion.rationale: Miasma Worm and similar variants masquerade as legitimate npm packages; pipeline should detect version tampering, metadata falsification, or package signature validation failures.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm audit and npm info output for warnings about unverified signatures, tampered metadata, or mismatched checksums. Flag installations of packages with suspiciously recent publish dates, zero documentation, or repositories pointing to non-GitHub/GitLab URLs.

suggestion.title: Initial Access — Fake Software Download / Browser Landing
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'spreads through fake websites that impersonate popular software, luring unsuspecting users into a trap.' No detection for suspicious browser activity landing on typosquatted domains (mlcrosoft.co.com, mlroweb.com pattern-matching).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect browser process initiating connections to defanged IOC domains (hebsbsbzjsjshduxbs.xyz, qq-0732gwh22.com, mlcrosoft.co.com, mlroweb.com) or regex-matching typosquatted software domains. Correlation: if user downloads/executes file after landing, raise severity.

suggestion.title: Execution — Reaper Malware Process Launch / Unsigned Binary
suggestion.rationale: Article describes malware called 'Reaper' with specific hashes (6552824c59ddacb134073f24a4bd4724514a938a9dc59f1733503642faed3bd3, c917fcf8314228862571f80c9e4a871e). No process execution detection for these hashes or unsigned/renamed browser/software impostors launching.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation matching hash IOCs or process name mimicking browser/software names but signed by unexpected publisher. File path outside standard installation directories (e.g., /tmp, Downloads, Desktop on Mac).

suggestion.title: Lateral Process Access — Parent-Child Execution Chain (Fake Software → Browser)
suggestion.rationale: Article narrative implies fake software executable launches or injects into browser processes. Article states malware 'can silently drain everything'—implies lateral privilege/credential access pattern not covered by direct file access hunts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parent-child execution where suspicious/uncommon process spawns Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge subprocess. Or suspicious process opens handle to browser process with query/read permissions (e.g., OpenProcess(PROCESS_VM_READ)).

suggestion.title: Collection — High-Volume Credential Enumeration (Keychain/Password Manager Access)
suggestion.rationale: Article targets 'crypto wallets' and browser passwords, implying enumeration of Keychain (macOS) or password manager indices. File-level detection alone misses API-level reads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Rapid sequential reads of password manager / keychain data files, or unsuspected process calling Keychain APIs (macOS). Baseline normal password manager read patterns per user; alert on 10x+ reads in 1-minute window from non-browser process.

suggestion.title: C2 Communication — Outbound to SHub/Reaper Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article provides 4 C2/phishing domains but pipeline did not generate network hunt. Standard IOC template should include: connections to hebsbsbzjsjshduxbs.xyz, qq-0732gwh22.com, mlcrosoft.co.com, mlroweb.com from any process outside expected context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Outbound DNS/HTTPS to IOC domains. Elevated alert if source process is non-browser or source process is browser but destination is non-standard port/path. Monitor for POST/exfiltration patterns (large data to C2).

suggestion.title: IIS Web Shell File Creation in Web Root
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'custom web shell framework' deployment to IIS; article body explicitly signals web-shell-based persistence but pipeline captured zero UCs for file-creation detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for new file creation under IIS web root directories (C:\inetpub\wwwroot, app pools) with executable extensions (.aspx, .asp, .ashx, .jspx) or double-extensions. Correlate with IIS process identity or unusual w3wp.exe file I/O; exclude known deployment tooling and updates.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Child Process Spawned from IIS Worker Process
suggestion.rationale: Web shells execute commands via IIS worker process (w3wp.exe); article topic implies command execution capability. Pipeline missed T1059 execution detection entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected child process creation from w3wp.exe, especially cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or rare executables. Baseline IIS app pools and alert on out-of-band process trees; correlate with recent file creates in web directories.

suggestion.title: IIS Access Log Anomalies – Web Shell Parameter Injection
suggestion.rationale: Custom web shells receive commands via HTTP request parameters; article describes 'framework' implying sophisticated parameter handling. No HTTP-layer detection suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parse IIS access logs for suspicious URL patterns: request URIs containing encoded payloads (%, %3D, %20), parameter names like 'cmd', 'execute', 'shell', or requests with unusually long query strings to newly-created ASPX files. Flag GET/POST to non-standard application paths.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement via IIS Application Credentials
suggestion.rationale: IIS servers often hold credentials in web.config; article title mentions 'targets Microsoft IIS' suggesting lateral movement from web tier. No credential-access UC generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for read access to web.config, applicationHost.config, and .NET credential stores (e.g., via web.config parser, IIS Manager modules). Alert on unusual process reading IIS configuration outside of normal W3SVC service lifecycle.

suggestion.title: Outbound C2 Communication from IIS Process
suggestion.rationale: Web shells exfiltrate data and receive commands over network; article implies C2 callback capability but no network-layer detection offered.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) network destinations; alert on new outbound connections to non-whitelisted IPs/domains, especially on non-standard ports (8080, 8443, 4444) or to suspicious ASNs. Flag DNS queries from IIS process for known DGA/C2 domains.

suggestion.title: IIS HttpModules or HttpHandlers Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Sophisticated IIS attacks install custom modules or handlers for persistence; 'custom framework' suggests advanced IIS instrumentation beyond simple file upload.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor web.config and applicationHost.config for new <modules> or <handlers> entries pointing to unsigned or recently-created DLLs. Alert on Registry changes to HKLM\Software\Microsoft\InetStp\Components. Correlate with file create events.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Process Execution on Cloud Instances
suggestion.rationale: Article states PCPJack hijacked 230 servers across AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. Compromised instances must execute attacker-controlled processes for C2 and relay operations; pipeline missed execution-phase detections entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected process spawning from system services, new binary locations, or child processes of init/systemd on cloud VMs. Flag SYSTEM/root-privilege execution of PowerShell, Bash, or curl from non-standard parent processes.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized SMTP Service Enablement and Relay Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes a 'Covert SMTP Relay Network'—hijacked servers actively relaying mail. Pipeline should detect SMTP service installation, unusual SMTP traffic egress, or mail queueing on compromised instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect schtasks/systemctl enabling sendmail, postfix, or exim on Windows/Linux cloud instances. Correlate with outbound TCP 25/587/2525 traffic and volume anomalies in mail logs (thousands of messages from single instance).

suggestion.title: Cloud Credential Compromise and Mass Instance Hijacking
suggestion.rationale: 230 servers across three cloud platforms indicates coordinated compromise via shared credentials, exploited config management, or lateral pivoting. Pipeline missed IAM/identity anomalies entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for bulk creation of IAM users, access keys, or service accounts. Detect cross-account role assumption, modified security groups/firewall rules, or instances launched in suspicious regions coinciding with account compromise time.

suggestion.title: Malware Persistence via Scheduled Tasks or Cron
suggestion.rationale: PCPJack must survive instance reboot cycles and OS updates to maintain SMTP relay operation across 230 servers. Pipeline did not identify persistence-phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag new Windows scheduled tasks or Linux cron jobs created within hours of instance compromise, especially those executing from /tmp, appdata, or attacker-controlled S3/blob storage paths.

suggestion.title: Command and Control Callback Detection
suggestion.rationale: PCPJack requires C2 channel for relay command issuance, updates, and server status reporting. Pipeline did not generate detections for beacon traffic or DNS exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect periodic outbound DNS queries or TCP connections from compromised instances to rare external IPs on non-standard ports. Look for regular-interval beaconing (every 5–15 minutes), high-entropy subdomain queries, or DNS requests matching known C2 patterns.

suggestion.title: Suspicious GitHub Actions Workflow Execution by Agentic AI
suggestion.rationale: Article context: 'Claude Code Github action case' directly implies detection of unauthorized or anomalous AI-driven workflow execution. Article establishes threat of agentic AI autonomously running commands in CI/CD.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect GitHub Actions runs triggered by AI agents (Claude Code) that execute shell commands outside expected repository-owner-initiated workflows. Flag runs with unusual env vars (e.g., ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, secrets injection), commands that spawn subshells or fetch external payloads, or runs from IP ranges not matching developer geolocation history.

suggestion.title: Exfiltration of Secrets from GitHub Actions Environment
suggestion.rationale: Article title references 'Securing CI/CD' implies threat model includes credential theft. Agentic AI in actions can access GITHUB_TOKEN, SSH keys, cloud creds. No UC extracted despite this being core attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for API calls from GitHub Actions workflows that query secrets managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) or read GITHUB_TOKEN/SSH_KEY environment variables followed by outbound HTTP/DNS to non-whitelisted domains.
