suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks often pivot through leaked credentials. '73 repositories' scale suggests either shared infrastructure compromise or token harvesting. Pipeline should detect abnormal token usage patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on GitHub API token usage from non-standard clients, unusual geographies, or API calls inconsistent with token owner's role (e.g., admin actions from read-only token). Flag tokens accessing >10 repositories in 24 hours.

suggestion.title: Sideloaded Android App Installation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly references malware distributed via 'Fake News, PDF and War Map Apps'—masqueraded as legitimate applications to drive installation. Title establishes app-as-vector but pipeline captured nothing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for installation of APK files from non-standard sources (Downloads folder, email attachments, WebView). Flag app installation events where package name contains lookalike strings (e.g., 'news', 'pdf', 'map' with typos or suffixes). Correlate against Google Play signatures.

suggestion.title: Excessive Android App Permission Requests
suggestion.rationale: Spyware classification ('Asin Targets Arabic Users') implies data collection—requires permissions for contacts, location, call logs, message access. Pipeline did not surface permission-granting as a detection vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on app permission grants for PERMISSION_ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS, READ_CALL_LOG, READ_SMS, RECORD_AUDIO when granted to applications with recent install dates or non-standard publisher certificates. Baseline expected permissions per app category.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Network Beaconing from App UIDs
suggestion.rationale: Spyware must exfiltrate collected data; article title implies collection of sensitive data from Arabic users. Pipeline omitted command-and-control detection despite 'spyware' classification.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network traffic initiated by recently-installed or suspicious app UIDs for unusual patterns: C2-like domains (low reputation, newly registered, no legitimate sinkhole history), suspicious ports (non-standard for app category), high-frequency beaconing, or encrypted tunnels to unknown ASNs.

suggestion.title: Malicious App Binary Obfuscation & Entropy
suggestion.rationale: Android spyware typically employs packing/obfuscation to evade static analysis. Article provides no IOCs (signature hashes, domains); pipeline should have flagged when these are absent but threat is confirmed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: On app installation, compute entropy of DEX sections and native libraries. Flag entropy >7.5 (high obfuscation) combined with app requesting sensitive permissions. Cross-reference against known packers (UPX, YGuard, ProGuard anomalies).

suggestion.title: Exfiltration of Contact & Geolocation Data
suggestion.rationale: Spyware explicitly targets users for data collection; article should enumerate what is stolen (contacts, location, messages, call history). Pipeline generated zero collection-phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect bulk reads from contacts database (ContentProvider queries to com.android.contacts) or GPS location APIs (FusedLocationProvider, LocationManager) followed by network writes to non-standard endpoints. Correlate timing and volume with known C2 intervals.

suggestion.title: Brickstorm Backdoor C2 Activity Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states Brickstorm 'undetected in environments of various targets...for more than a year.' Describes it as 'advanced malware implant' with Golang and Rust variants. Specifically notes researchers 'created a fingerprint to identify IP addresses and domains Brickstorm used for C2 communication' and deployed to Egnyte, pfSense, Linux systems. Phrase: 'Between September 18 and September 23, all of the servers previously matching this pattern turned off their services on port 443.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for WebSocket protocol anomalies on non-standard ports from infrastructure appliances (Egnyte, Synology, firewall) without EDR; fingerprint Brickstorm's TLS certificate/cipher suite patterns observed during investigation; correlate successful Golang/Rust process execution on infrastructure with outbound HTTPS connections to known C2 infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Plenet/.NET Backdoor Execution on NAS Appliances
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies Plenet as 'cross-platform .NET-based backdoor' offering 'interactive shell access, remote command execution, file manipulation' and states 'deployed the custom malware Plenet to a Synology NAS appliance' after re-establishing access. Notes it uses 'WebSocket protocol for C2 communications and a multiplexing library for simultaneous data streams.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on .NET assembly execution or loading on Synology/Linux-based appliances (anomalous for patched systems); detect WebSocket library imports (System.Net.WebSockets) compiled into executables on infrastructure; monitor SSH/Telnet sessions spawning shells or downloading binaries to NAS devices.

suggestion.title: SSL VPN Firewall Configuration Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'used stolen credentials to enable and configure SSL VPN access on the victim's firewall' and deployed Brickstorm to MSP's pfSense firewall compromised 'at least 18 months earlier.' Represents infrastructure-level persistence mechanism distinct from endpoint malware.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect firewall administrative access and SSL VPN configuration changes outside maintenance windows using historical baselines; alert on new VPN user accounts created with non-standard naming or linked to compromised credentials; monitor for firewall certificate replacements or route modifications following access logs from multiple IP geographies.

suggestion.title: Conditional Access Policy Evasion via Proxy Relaying
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Volexity assesses with high confidence that this was done to blend in with legitimate network traffic and evade Conditional Access policies' using Brickstorm's 'proxying features' to access Microsoft 365. Attackers used 'stolen credentials' through this proxy layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate M365 sign-in events originating from homogeneous source IPs (internal VPN) with impossible-travel patterns or ASN mismatches; detect successful Conditional Access exemptions or policy modifications; monitor for sign-in anomalies (unusual time-of-day, geo, user-agent) immediately following Brickstorm C2 activity windows.

suggestion.title: Multi-Vector Infrastructure Compromise Detection
suggestion.rationale: Attack spans appliance types: 'Egnyte Storage Sync system...accessed it periodically through the victim's web SSL VPN,' then 'deployed additional custom malware to a Synology NAS device' and 'Brickstorm was then deployed to the victim's Egnyte Storage Sync appliance and to a retired Linux GroupWise email archive server.' Targets 'systems that do not support endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for malware staging/deployment chains across heterogeneous infrastructure (storage, firewall, NAS, archive servers); detect living-off-the-land tool usage (curl, wget, bash, ssh) to download payloads to systems assumed to have minimal access controls; baseline legitimate file writes to appliances and alert on suspicious binary/script creation.

suggestion.title: AgentPSD Python Reverse Shell Fallback Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies AgentPSD as 'simple Python-based reverse shell utility' deployed as 'fallback persistence mechanism if other malware was no longer accessible' and 'configured to connect to a different domain than the one Brickstorm used.' Indicates intentional redundancy in persistence strategy.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Python interpreter (python.exe, python3, python2.7) with network socket operations or subprocess spawning (/bin/bash, cmd.exe); monitor for scheduled persistence (crontab entries, Windows scheduled tasks) executing Python scripts; correlate AgentPSD C2 domain connections with secondary ASN or geolocation distinct from primary Brickstorm infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Detect HTTP POST with Content-Encoding: deflate to Serv-U Services
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'specially crafted POST requests that crash the Serv-U service without authentication using Content-Encoding: deflate.' This is the attack signature; detection baseline is mandatory.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP POST requests bearing Content-Encoding: deflate headers to known or discovered Serv-U ports (2121, 3000, 8080, or responsive banners). Correlate with Serv-U error/crash logs. False positives unlikely; header+port combination is strong signal.

suggestion.title: Detect Serv-U Service Termination Following Exploit Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'crash the Serv-U service without authentication.' Service crash is the direct impact; process termination events are observable on Windows/Linux endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected ServeU.exe or servu process termination, especially preceded by HTTP anomalies. Track restart frequency; repeated crashes in short windows indicate active exploitation.

suggestion.title: Asset Inventory: Vulnerable Serv-U Service Discovery
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Shodan currently tracks over 12,000 Serv-U servers exposed online.' Requires continuous asset discovery and version baseline to target patching.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan for Serv-U service identification via banner grabbing, port enumeration (default 2121/FTP, 3000/HTTP), and version detection. Flag instances running Serv-U <15.5.4 Hotfix 1. Cross-reference with exposure feeds (Shodan, Censys).

suggestion.title: Detect Exploitation of Historical Serv-U Flaws (CVE-2021-35211, CVE-2024-28995)
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Clop ransomware gang exploited...CVE-2021-35211' and 'CVE-2024-28995...actively exploited.' Threat actors recycle proven exploits; parallel detection reduces risk.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create rules for known exploitation signatures: path-traversal sequences in Serv-U URIs (CVE-2024-28995), RCE payloads in multipart/POST bodies (CVE-2021-35211). Test for polyglot exploitation chains targeting multiple CVEs sequentially.

suggestion.title: Monitor for Ransomware Reconnaissance on Serv-U Assets
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'ransomware gangs have targeted vulnerabilities in Serv-U.' Clop used CVE-2021-35211 for network breach. Serv-U access suggests lateral movement or data exfiltration intent post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag successful Serv-U authentication from unusual IP/user contexts. Monitor for data staging (large files in Serv-U directories), archive creation, or credential enumeration post-compromise of Serv-U server.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U POST Request with Content-Encoding Deflate
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'specially crafted POST requests using the Content-Encoding: deflate header' as the specific exploitation technique. This is the precise attack vector and should be detectable as HTTP anomaly or DoS attempt signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor inbound HTTP POST requests to Serv-U endpoints with 'Content-Encoding: deflate' header from untrusted sources. Correlate with Serv-U service restart/crash events occurring within 5-30 seconds. Unpatched systems vulnerable to CVE-2026-28318 are primary targets.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U Unexpected Service Termination
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states vulnerability 'crash[es] the Serv-U service without authentication.' Service crashes are the observable impact and indicate exploitation attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected Serv-U service terminations, especially those preceded by POST requests or HTTP errors. Track mean-time-between-crashes (MTBC) for unpatched instances. Post-2026-06-05, sustained crashes in unpatched systems strongly indicate active exploitation.

suggestion.title: Unpatched SolarWinds Serv-U Asset Inventory Query
suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV entry with federal remediation deadline 2026-06-19. Asset discovery and patch-status inventory are mandatory for KEV; article emphasizes patch-lag exposure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query patch management systems and vulnerability scanners for SolarWinds Serv-U versions prior to CVE-2026-28318 fix. Prioritize internet-facing instances by cross-referencing firewall rules and network segmentation data. Flag all accessible, unpatched assets for emergency remediation before federal deadline.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-28318 Vulnerability Scan Hit Correlation
suggestion.rationale: CVE-2026-28318 is the IOC identifier for this KEV entry. Standard vulnerability-scanning and threat-intel correlation should detect and flag all affected assets.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Match CVE-2026-28318 against all active vulnerability scans and threat-intel feeds. Correlate with patch-status records. Escalate any unpatched matches to security teams with priority commensurate to network exposure. Retroactively hunt incident logs from 2026-06-05 onwards for signs of exploitation (service crashes, POST anomalies, Denial of Service) on unpatched systems.

suggestion.title: vScript Tenant Upload Command Injection Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article provides explicit log pattern: 'Tenant list upload per vsmart serial number: /usr/bin/vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh -cli path /home/admin/malicious.csv vpn 0'. This is the attack execution and should trigger alerts on suspicious script invocation with file path parameters.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor /var/log/scripts.log for vconfd_script_upload_tenant_list.sh invocations with suspicious file paths (e.g., /home/admin/*, non-standard locations). Alert on any tenant configuration upload attempts when the calling account is not expected administrator service accounts.

suggestion.title: Malicious File Upload to SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by uploading a crafted file to the affected system.' Requires detection of abnormal file uploads to vManage instances, especially to paths like /home/admin/.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect file uploads to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager vManage instances targeting administrative directories (/home/admin/, configuration paths). Correlate with subsequent /var/log/scripts.log entries. Alert if upload precedes script execution within 10 minutes.

suggestion.title: Privilege Escalation via vconfd Root Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'a successful exploit could allow the attacker to perform command injection attacks and elevate their privileges as the root user.' Need detection of processes executing with elevated privileges after vconfd_script_upload invocation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child processes spawned by vconfd or vScript services running as root (UID 0) immediately following tenant configuration uploads. Alert if non-system accounts initiate root-level operations via vconfd mechanisms.

suggestion.title: Configuration Push to SD-WAN Edge Devices Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'Cisco has observed limited cases where the exploitation of this bug resulted in a configuration change pushed to edge devices.' Requires detection of unauthorized config distributions to managed Catalyst devices.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor vManage configuration push logs for unexpected changes to edge device configurations (vSmart serial numbers listed in push commands). Alert on config pushes initiated outside normal maintenance windows or by accounts not in admin groups.

suggestion.title: Authentication Bypass Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-20182 / CVE-2026-20127)
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'To exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have netadmin privileges...This would require valid credentials or exploitation of CVE-2026-20182 or CVE-2026-20127.' Need detection of these predecessor CVEs as indicators of CVE-2026-20245 attack prep.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-20182 (max-severity auth bypass) and CVE-2026-20127 (critical auth bypass active since 2023). Look for unauthenticated API calls, JWT token manipulation, or controller access logs with unexpected privilege grants. Flag as high-risk if followed by file uploads or vScript execution.

suggestion.title: Netadmin Privilege Acquisition Without Auth Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Article states privilege escalation requires 'valid credentials or exploitation of CVE-2026-20182/20127.' Should detect anomalous netadmin account creation or privilege grant that may bypass the auth-bypass chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor vManage user/role management logs for sudden netadmin role grants to service or unexpected accounts. Alert on privilege escalation attempts that don't correlate with CVE-2026-20182/20127 exploitation, suggesting direct credential compromise.

suggestion.title: Suspicious World Cup Phishing Domain Registration
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Fake Sites' targeting World Cup fans; pipeline extracted zero domains. Detection should flag newly registered or lookalike domains using World Cup 2026, FIFA, or tournament-related keywords.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS queries and web requests to domains registered within 30 days containing 'world-cup', 'fifa2026', 'tournament' keywords. Correlate with WHOIS privacy flags and bulk registrations. Baseline against legitimate FIFA/tournament domains.

suggestion.title: Banking Malware Execution from World Cup-Themed Attachment
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'Banking Malware' but pipeline generated no execution-phase detections. Expect email-borne delivery disguised as tickets, registration links.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect process execution (exe, dll, script) spawned from user temp folders or Downloads following email open. Look for banking malware process names (zeus, emotet variants) or unusual child processes from Excel/Word macros. Correlate with email attachment names containing 'ticket', 'registration', 'final'.

suggestion.title: Credential Access from World Cup Phishing Campaign
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'Stolen Logins'; no credential access detections proposed. Need to identify bulk login attempts using harvested credentials.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on high-velocity failed login attempts followed by success using credentials matching World Cup phishing target usernames. Flag logins from IP ranges inconsistent with target organization geography. Detect password spray patterns across FIFA ticketing partner domains.

suggestion.title: Money Transfer Anomaly Post-Credential Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article states scams target financial accounts; impact phase should detect unusual transfers. Pipeline missed this critical harm indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual fund transfers (amount, frequency, destination) within 2-4 hours of World Cup phishing email open or credential compromise confirmation. Flag transfers to newly-added beneficiaries or offshore accounts during tournament period.

suggestion.title: World Cup-Themed Malicious File Hash Detection
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline output contains no file hashes despite 'Banking Malware' in title. Require hash correlation against phishing payloads and banking trojans.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference executable file hashes extracted from World Cup phishing campaign against known banking malware signatures (Zeus, Emotet, QBot families). Alert on first-seen binaries with FIFA/tournament metadata in file properties executed post-email delivery.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Geographic Login Post-Phishing
suggestion.rationale: Scam targets international audience; credential misuse should show impossible-travel patterns. Pipeline generated no detection for this.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag successful logins from geographic regions inconsistent with user baseline within 6 hours of phishing email delivery. Combine with impossible-travel (login distance > 900km in <1 hour). Increase fidelity by correlating VPN/proxy bypass indicators.

suggestion.title: DbGate unauthenticated RCE — POST /runners/start code injection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'JSON script runner (POST /runners/start) allows remote code execution via code injection in the functionName parameter.' This is the primary exploitation entry point and should be hunted at the network level.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor POST requests to /runners/start endpoint from external sources without valid authentication tokens. Flag payloads containing JSON assign commands with suspicious functionName values containing shell metacharacters (|, &, ;, >, $, backticks) or template-string patterns (${...}).

suggestion.title: Node.js child process spawning shells — DbGate exploit execution
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'generated code is then executed in a forked Node.js child process.' Exploitation immediately leads to process spawning; this is the execution-phase detection opportunity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on Node.js (node, node.exe) spawning shell interpreters (bash, sh, powershell.exe, cmd.exe) or data-exfil tools (curl, wget, nc). Correlate parent process to dbgate-related paths (.dbgate/run/*, bundle.js, DBGATE_API env var) or process cmdline.

suggestion.title: System binary persistence writes from DbGate execution
suggestion.rationale: Subprocess execution context from code injection creates opportunity for attacker to persist via filesystem writes to system binary directories. Not explicitly described but is a natural exploitation continuation vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor FileCreated or FileModified events in /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/local/sbin when initiated by Node.js process or its children spawned from DbGate execution context.

suggestion.title: DbGate /runners/load-reader secondary exploit entry point
suggestion.rationale: Article description of vulnerabilities references both /runners/start and /runners/load-reader endpoints as injectable surfaces. Second entry point should have distinct detection rule.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag POST requests to /runners/load-reader from external sources, especially payloads with unusual JSON nesting depth, large request bodies (>10KB), or embedded encoded strings that may contain obfuscated JavaScript.

suggestion.title: DbGate unauthenticated authentication endpoint exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'the none auth provider issues JWT tokens without credentials via POST /auth/login, so this is exploitable by any netw...' This is the initial access vector and should be independently detectable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect POST requests to /auth/login endpoints on DbGate instances with response codes indicating successful token issuance (200/201) without corresponding authentication headers or credentials in the request body. Correlate with known DbGate ports (default 3000) and User-Agent patterns typical of automated tooling.

suggestion.title: Suspicious ZIP extraction with path traversal indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article describes core vulnerability: 'unzipDirectory() function...does not validate that extracted file paths stay within the output directory. A malicious ZIP with ../ entries writes files anywhere.' Requires detection of ZIP upload/extraction with traversal sequences.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for node process calling unzip or extract operations on archives containing path segments with '/../' or '..\' sequences in archived filenames. Alert when extraction target directory differs from declared output directory, or when extracted file count exceeds uploaded ZIP's expected contents count.

suggestion.title: Web shell persistence via OS-sensitive file writes post-extraction
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates 'persistence...via web shell' (T1505.003) as viable outcome. Attack writes to web-accessible directories (e.g., /var/www, application root) to persist code execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect node process (DbGate) writing .php, .jsp, .py, or .sh files to web-accessible directories (/var/www, /app/public, etc.) immediately following ZIP extraction operations. Correlate with subsequent HTTP requests to those newly-created paths.

suggestion.title: Privilege escalation artifacts: sudoers and SSH key modification
suggestion.rationale: Article states default deployment 'runs as root' and vulnerability allows 'writes files anywhere on filesystem,' including /etc/sudoers.d, /root/.ssh (shown in UC_23_2 paths). These enable privilege escalation (T1548) or lateral movement.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on modifications to /etc/sudoers, /etc/sudoers.d/*, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, or /root/.ssh/config by non-standard processes. Since DbGate already runs as root, focus on TIMESTAMPS: extract operation followed by permission/ownership change to those files within seconds indicates exploitation, not admin activity.

suggestion.title: Defender network anomaly: incoming DbGate archive uploads from untrusted sources
suggestion.rationale: Exploitation requires uploading a crafted malicious ZIP. Article lacks details on expected upload locations but /api/archive/unzip and /api/archive/save-uploaded-zip suggest file upload endpoints. Baseline legitimate traffic first.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of legitimate ZIP uploads to DbGate instances (size, frequency, source subnets). Alert on uploads >5MB (suspicious complexity for normal use), from external IP ranges, with rapid subsequent extraction operations, or from IPs flagged as malicious in threat intel.

suggestion.title: DbGate /runners/load-reader POST with functionName parameter abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'unsanitized functionName parameter in /runners/load-reader endpoint.' This is the direct vector and should be the primary detection hook, not a secondary indicator search.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: POST requests to /runners/load-reader with functionName parameter containing code injection markers (newline characters, dynamic import statements, child_process requires) indicate exploitation attempts. Baseline on legitimate DbGate administrative traffic first.

suggestion.title: Dynamic import() abuse in Node.js application context
suggestion.rationale: Article states the 'require = null mitigation is trivially bypassed via dynamic import().' This is a core evasion technique and warrants dedicated detection for JavaScript runtime analysis.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for import() calls in contexts where require() is forbidden/null, particularly in request handlers. Correlate with suspicious process spawning afterward.

suggestion.title: Authenticated DbGate session followed by /runners/load-reader POST
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes this is 'authenticated RCE'—requires valid credentials. Baseline legitimate admin sessions, then alert on authenticated users accessing /runners/load-reader who do not normally do so.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify baseline users and their typical access patterns to DbGate. Flag anomalous /runners/load-reader requests from legitimate accounts, especially followed by process execution or shell spawning.

suggestion.title: Node.js child_process module invocation from HTTP request handler
suggestion.rationale: The attack injects code that spawns shell commands. Detection should look for child_process.exec/spawn/execSync calls initiated from HTTP request context, a strong indicator of injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child_process invocations from within HTTP request handlers or asynchronous callbacks tied to HTTP endpoints. Correlate with /runners/load-reader or similar DbGate API endpoints.

suggestion.title: File write to unexpected paths via ait-bsc or Python process
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states BSC 'blindly trusts path-related form fields' and 'direct BSC to log to arbitrary filesystem paths.' Detection should trigger on anomalous file writes issued by the BSC process to paths outside the configured log root (e.g., /etc/, /var/spool/, user home directories, /tmp).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor file creation/modification events where InitiatingProcessFileName matches ait-bsc or python* and the target file path does not match the baseline BSC log directory (typically /var/opt/ait-bsc/logs or configured in bsc.yaml). Flag writes to /etc/, /home/, /tmp/, /var/spool/cron, or paths containing .. or symlinks.

suggestion.title: HTTP POST to BSC /<name>/start with missing or null path parameters
suggestion.rationale: Article describes the vulnerability as path-traversal injection via 'form fields'; attacker supplies malicious log_dir_path, file_name_pattern, or path parameters. Detection should also flag requests with NULL, empty, or missing parameters (e.g., log_dir_path= with no value), which may indicate fuzzing or bypass attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on POST to /<handler>/start where the URI query string contains parameter names (log_dir_path, file_name_pattern, path) but values are empty, null, or contain only whitespace. Combine with lack of authorization headers to confirm unauthenticated access.

suggestion.title: Configuration file reads before BSC handler creation
suggestion.rationale: To exploit the vulnerability, attacker must know or guess the current log root directory. Article states 'Bypass the configured log root'—implying prior reconnaissance. Detection should correlate reads of bsc.yaml or BSC config files with subsequent POST to /start endpoint.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect file-open or read events for bsc.yaml, bsc.conf, or other BSC config files, followed within 60 seconds by an HTTP POST to /<name>/start from the same source IP, especially if unauthenticated.

suggestion.title: Symlink or hardlink writes via path-traversal payload
suggestion.rationale: If attacker writes to paths such as /etc/passwd, /var/spool/cron/crontabs, or other sensitive locations, they may attempt to overwrite or append to symlink targets. Article says 'arbitrary file append'—suggesting attacker appends malicious content. Detect file writes to symlink-embedded paths or suspicious modifications to setuid/world-writable files.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag file-write events where the target path resolves through a symlink, or where the target is a known privileged file (/etc/sudoers, /etc/crontab, /root/.ssh, /var/spool/cron) and the writing process is ait-bsc or Python.

suggestion.title: Rapid role creation followed by administrator user deletion
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'create new roles and delete other users, including administrators' — this sequential exploitation pattern (role creation → admin deletion) is the actual attack, not just endpoint access. Endpoint detection alone cannot distinguish from legitimate admin activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect a single authenticated user creating one or more new roles AND deleting at least one high-privilege user (admin, owner, moderator) within 15 minutes via Livewire endpoints. Establish baseline of normal admin role-creation frequency; alert on non-admin users or out-of-hours sequences. Require correlation with /settings/team/index access in HTTP logs.

suggestion.title: Privilege escalation correlated with team-settings endpoint access
suggestion.rationale: Article describes vulnerability resulting in 'take over the RBAC system' — the privilege elevation from authenticated user to admin is the exploitation artifact and should be detected via ACL/audit log changes paired with endpoint access timing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when a user account gains admin, owner, or moderator role assignment within 10 minutes of first accessing /settings/team/index or /settings/team/rolePermission endpoints. Prioritize accounts whose prior role was 'user', 'guest', or non-privileged. Correlate with user not in documented change-management schedule or requesting their own role elevation.

suggestion.title: High-privilege account deletion by non-administrator
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly calls out 'delete other users, including administrators' as the exploitation impact — admin account deletion by non-admin context is a clear indicator of compromised RBAC or authorization bypass and requires immediate alerting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on ANY deletion or disablement of users assigned admin, owner, or moderator roles. Flag if the deleting user lacks admin privileges or has role level below the deleted account. Correlate with /settings/team endpoint access within 30 minutes prior. Escalate to critical if admin account is deleted and then restored within 1 hour (rollback indicator).

suggestion.title: WordPress Plugin RCE via Exploit Public-Facing Application
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'hackers exploit critical...flaw to take over sites' — this is the initial attack vector. Pipeline extracted zero initial_access detections despite clear exploitation narrative.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP POST/GET requests to Everest Forms plugin endpoints (/wp-content/plugins/everest-forms/) with suspicious payloads, serialized PHP objects, or SQL injection syntax. Flag requests returning 200 OK followed by web shell creation within seconds.

suggestion.title: PHP Code Execution via Web Server Process
suggestion.rationale: Site takeover requires arbitrary code execution. Article confirms compromise but pipeline missed execution phase detections common in WordPress RCE.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect PHP interpreter spawning shell (apache/nginx/www-data user invoking bash/sh). Monitor for file creation in /wp-content/uploads/ or /wp-content/plugins/ by www-data user, especially .php files created outside normal update windows.

suggestion.title: WordPress Admin Account Creation Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Site takeover requires persistence; attackers create rogue admin account. Article's 'take over' implies sustained access but pipeline missed credential/persistence detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor wp_users table for INSERT events or WordPress admin.php logs for new user_register actions. Alert on accounts created outside business hours, with suspicious usernames (admin2, wp-admin, administrator), or from non-standard IP addresses.

suggestion.title: Backdoor Plugin Installation
suggestion.rationale: Attackers typically install malicious plugin post-RCE for persistent access. Article confirms 'take over' (ongoing access) but pipeline missed plugin persistence detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on new directories created under /wp-content/plugins/ followed by .php file creation within seconds, especially with obfuscated or base64-encoded content. Cross-reference with backdoor signatures and YARA rules.

suggestion.title: Web Shell Upload to Uploads Directory
suggestion.rationale: Alternative persistence vector. Article confirms site takeover but pipeline missed detection of executable uploads to writable WordPress directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor /wp-content/uploads/ for .php, .phtml, .phar file creation. Flag uploads containing eval(), system(), passthru(), or base64_decode() when decoded. Alert on files uploaded via POST to wp-admin or plugin handler endpoints.

suggestion.title: WordPress Configuration File Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Attackers modify wp-config.php or htaccess for backdoor activation or credential harvesting. Article indicates full site compromise but pipeline missed config-modification detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for modifications to wp-config.php, .htaccess, wp-settings.php outside maintenance windows. Alert on addition of new database credentials, FTP details, or define() calls for backdoor triggers. Compare file hashes against known-good WordPress distributions.

suggestion.title: Malicious PyPI Package Installed: parsimonius (Typosquatted)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'parsimonius' crafted to mimic 'parsimonious' with a single missing letter, installed by developers. Pipeline generated zero use cases despite this being the primary execution vector: 'a deceptive Python package quietly made its way into the PyPI repository.' Initial-access and execution phases are narrative-present but undetected.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor pip install operations and package manager logs for installation of 'parsimonius' or other single-character deviations from legitimate PyPI packages (parsimonious, requests, urllib3, etc.). Correlate with new/unsigned packages and minimal download history. Flag developer workstations and CI/CD runners.

suggestion.title: File Hash IOC Match: Malicious Python Package Artifact
suggestion.rationale: SHA1 a01c2a21f24db63cb01a67016519aebeca438089 is present in article IOC section but completely absent from pipeline IOC output (returned as empty dict). This is a direct extraction failure, not an analytical gap. Standard hash-matching hunt was not synthesized despite being mentioned in recommended hunts template.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Match SHA1 a01c2a21f24db63cb01a67016519aebeca438089 against file events and process hashes. Priority on Python site-packages directories, interpreter processes, and package manager write operations. High confidence alert on any hit.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Python Code Execution from New Package Import
suggestion.rationale: Malicious package installation inherently leads to code execution when imported or on install-time (post-install scripts). Article states package 'put thousands of developers at risk' implying execution occurred. No behavioral detection for post-install or import-time execution was suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate pip install or package download of suspicious/newly-published packages with subsequent Python subprocess creation, network I/O, or file exfiltration. Flag installations followed by network beacons, credential access, or process spawning within 60 seconds.

suggestion.title: PyPI Typosquatting Attack: Package Name Similarity to Legitimate Library
suggestion.rationale: Core attack vector is supply-chain compromise via typosquatting: 'a deceptive Python package...crafted to look almost identical to the widely used parsimonious library. The single missing letter was no...' Pipeline did not surface T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise or generate typosquatting-specific detection logic despite this being the sole attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag PyPI package downloads where package name has edit distance 1–2 from known legitimate libraries (parsimonious, requests, cryptography, etc.). Prioritize newly-published packages (first-seen < 7 days), unsigned/unverified signatures, and minimal star/fork history. Cross-reference against corporate package allowlists.

suggestion.title: Trusted installer bundling unexpected payload binaries
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states the compromise 'distributing an unexpected executable file alongside its legitimate installer' — me.exe was bundled with Hola setup.exe, but no detection rules hunt for installers that drop child executables with unusual names or hashes to temp/appdata paths.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Installer processes (setup.exe, installer.exe) creating or extracting unexpected .exe files outside their expected subdirectories. Look for parent-child process relationships where legitimate browser/app installer spawns executables with cryptominer-typical names (me.exe, miner.exe) or paths indicating temp extraction.

suggestion.title: Cryptominer behavioral hunt — sustained high CPU + network to mining pools
suggestion.rationale: Article characterizes payload as cryptominer but provides no behavioral detection rule. me.exe would exhibit sustained CPU spikes (>70%) and outbound connections to mining pool CIDR ranges; standard IOC-driven hunts miss active mining behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Processes with low privilege and no user interaction showing sustained CPU utilization >70% for extended periods (>1hr continuously) combined with outbound connections to known mining pool IP ranges (Monero, Ethereum, Bitcoin pools) or mining-pool domain registrations. Baseline CPU profiles to exclude legitimate background activity.

suggestion.title: Supply-chain installer hash blacklist + signature validation failure
suggestion.rationale: Four high-fidelity hashes (SHA256, SHA1, MD5) are provided. Detection should flag endpoints that downloaded or executed any of these exact binaries—this is higher-confidence than behavioral rules for supply-chain IOCs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: File creation, download, or process execution matching any of the four provided hashes (174086534a2de7..., e3541caf708c07..., SHA1 8046735d..., MD5 8462f61e...). Enrich with installer parent process (Hola Browser setup) and timestamp to confirm supply-chain vector.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated executable unpacking / process injection indicators (T1027 enforcement)
suggestion.rationale: Article lists T1027 (Obfuscated Files or Information) as a technique but no detection rule hunts for the runtime unpacking, code injection, or process hollowing that obfuscation implies. me.exe likely deobfuscates in memory.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: me.exe or child processes showing (a) sudden memory growth without corresponding file I/O, (b) LoadImage/CreateRemoteThread calls into system processes (rundll32, svchost, explorer), (c) API call sequences consistent with shellcode injection (VirtualAlloc → WriteProcessMemory → CreateRemoteThread). Baseline legitimate installers to reduce FP.

suggestion.title: Persistence mechanism installation by cryptominer payload (T1547 search)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes a cryptominer but provides no hunt for its persistence mechanisms. Cryptominers typically install startup shortcuts, scheduled tasks, or registry run keys. No detection rule covers post-install persistence by me.exe.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: me.exe or processes spawned by me.exe creating entries in HKLM/HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, modifications to startup folders (%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), or creation of scheduled tasks with suspicious cadence. Correlate with parent (installer) and timestamp.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Installation - Malicious Payload
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions malware 'hit npm' via 'supply chain attacks' — the attack vector is malicious npm package installation. No UC was generated despite this being the primary attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected process spawning from node/npm package install contexts (npm, yarn, pnpm). Flag executions of shell commands, curl/wget, or encoded PowerShell within installation hooks. Focus on post-install scripts and transitive dependencies downloading unsigned binaries.

suggestion.title: npm Registry Tampering - Package Version Manipulation
suggestion.rationale: Article title references 'New Miasma Worm Variant' suggests version substitution or typosquatting. No detection for registry anomalies or package manifest changes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on rapid consecutive package publishes to npm by same publisher. Flag publish events where package content (tarball hash, dependencies) changed without version bump. Detect orphaned/suspended accounts re-publishing packages.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated or Minified Code in node_modules - Supply Chain Malware
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain worms typically hide payloads in heavily obfuscated JavaScript. No UC for code-level detection. Article describes 'worm' — implies propagation code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest node_modules post-install; flag .js files with entropy >7.5 or >80% encoded/hex content. Detect commonjs require() calls to base64-decoded strings or eval(). Track first-seen obfuscated packages against malware signatures.

suggestion.title: Outbound C2 from Node Package Installation Context
suggestion.rationale: Worms require command-and-control communication. Title mentions two distinct malware families, implying C2 infrastructure. No network-based detection suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline expected egress from npm installation (registry.npmjs.org). Flag unexpected DNS queries or HTTP(S) connections to known C2 or newly-registered domains during/immediately after package install. Detect DNS tunneling or DGA patterns.

suggestion.title: Cross-Package Dependency Chain Compromise Detection
suggestion.rationale: npm packages can transitively pull in malicious sub-dependencies. Article implies multiple malware variants (IronWorm, Miasma) — likely delivered via transitive dependency injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate installed package manifests (package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json) against a baseline. Alert when transitive dependencies include packages not explicitly listed in top-level package.json. Flag dependency resolution to older/yanked versions.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement via Compromised npm Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain foothold enables lateral movement to other projects. Article vagueness on scope suggests multi-project impact. No UC for credential-based propagation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm token/credential usage for anomalies: geo-shift in publish location, unusual package targets, publish events to previously-untouched namespaces. Flag publish from CI/CD systems outside normal maintenance windows.

suggestion.title: Asset exposure — DD-WRT devices vulnerable to Gafgyt exploits
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'exploits a stack buffer overflow flaw in the UPnP service of affected routers' targeting DD-WRT specifically. Pipeline output generated zero use cases despite listing 5 CVEs (CVE-2021-27137, CVE-2015-2051, CVE-2022-35914, CVE-2016-15047, CVE-2025-34054). Standard asset hunt template should be instantiated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query infrastructure for devices running DD-WRT firmware versions vulnerable to the listed CVEs, specifically checking UPnP service status and version inventory. Flag any exposed management interfaces.

suggestion.title: Network connections to Gafgyt C2 infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article lists three C2 IP addresses (85.215.131.70, 217.160.125.125, 176.100.37.91) but pipeline extracted zero network IOCs. Standard network IOC hunt template should be instantiated for outbound/inbound connections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect any internal hosts initiating connections to the three C2 IPs on any port. Malware likely beacons over HTTP/HTTPS or raw TCP. Monitor for both successful and failed connection attempts.

suggestion.title: Gafgyt variant C0XMO binary detection via hash matching
suggestion.rationale: Article provides 15 SHA256 file hashes for malware samples but pipeline output shows zero file IOCs extracted. Standard hash hunt template should be instantiated against endpoint telemetry.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query endpoint logs for process execution, file writes, or in-memory detections matching any of the 15 provided SHA256 hashes. Flag any matches as confirmed Gafgyt installation regardless of filename or path.

suggestion.title: UPnP stack buffer overflow exploitation attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article specifically describes 'stack buffer overflow flaw in the UPnP service' — this is the attack vector. Pipeline did not surface exploitation activity hunting despite T1190 being identified. Need behavioral detection for memory corruption attacks against UPnP.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor UPnP service logs for malformed request payloads, buffer overflow signatures, or unexpected code execution. Alert on any process spawned by UPnP daemon with abnormal parent-child relationship or privilege escalation.

suggestion.title: Modular malware loader staging and propagation
suggestion.rationale: Article title emphasizes 'Modular Propagation' and mentions the malware 'works to [...]' propagate. Pipeline generated no persistence or lateral movement hunts. Modular architecture implies secondary payload loading or peer-to-peer propagation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect compromised routers establishing outbound connections to non-standard ports or attempting to propagate to neighboring Linux systems. Monitor for HTTP/HTTPS requests downloading multiple binaries or shell commands executing network reconnaissance (nmap, arp-scan).

suggestion.title: Malicious JavaScript injection in payment checkout pages
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'malware has been discovered hiding inside one of the most trusted payment platforms.' Magecart attacks inject skimming code into checkout flows; pipeline missed this execution/persistence vector entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for script tags or inline JavaScript added to payment pages that reference external C2 domains or encode card data before submission. Baseline legitimate checkout scripts and alert on deviations that add DOM listeners to card input fields.

suggestion.title: Exfiltration of payment card data to untrusted endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'pointing stolen card data to [C2]' and 'data dump.' Pipeline shows zero exfiltration-phase detections despite this being the core attack objective.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor payment processor logs and network egress for card data (PAN, CVV patterns) being sent to non-whitelisted endpoints. Flag API calls that collect card data then immediately transmit it external to payment network.

suggestion.title: Abuse of Stripe/payment-service APIs for command-and-control
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: 'uses Stripe...as both its command center and its data dump.' No C2 detection generated; this is a novel evasion technique using a trusted service as the C2 channel.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate Stripe API calls from unusual source IPs with corresponding data exfiltration events. Look for API metadata fields (user_agent, source_ip) being modified post-payment, or webhooks being created to external domains. Baseline normal Stripe API patterns for each merchant.

suggestion.title: Domain impersonation of legitimate payment services
suggestion.rationale: IOC 'braintree-payment-app.firebaseio.com' masquerades as Braintree (a real payment provider). Pipeline listed the domain but did not flag masquerading as a technique or detection angle.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on domains that mimic legitimate payment service names (Stripe, Braintree, PayPal, Square) hosted on infrastructure outside official vendors. Cross-reference WHOIS registration domain with company ownership and registration date patterns of known Magecart infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Suspicious enrollment or modification of Stripe webhooks
suggestion.rationale: Attack uses Stripe as 'command center'; this implies webhook abuse or API token exfiltration to receive C2 commands. No UC captures this lateral movement or persistence mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Stripe webhook creation/deletion logs for unusual endpoints. Alert if webhooks are added pointing to non-merchant infrastructure. Cross-correlate with failed authentication attempts or API key resets.

suggestion.title: Payment page HTML/DOM anomalies indicating malware presence
suggestion.rationale: Magecart signature is unusual script additions to checkout flows. Article mentions 'hiding inside' payment platform but no behavioral/static detection suggested for the malware artifact itself.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline legitimate checkout page DOM and JavaScript libraries. Alert on exfiltrated page source that includes base64-encoded strings, obfuscated variables referencing 'card', 'cvv', or 'pan', or new external script imports added after deployment.

suggestion.title: IIS Suspicious Script Upload or Creation
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly describes 'Custom Web Shell Framework' deployed to IIS—core persistence mechanism. Article should detail upload paths, script extensions, or behavioral markers of shell deployment that pipeline completely missed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor IIS application directories (wwwroot, virtual dirs) for unexpected .aspx, .jsp, .php, or .ashx file creation with suspicious modification times or execution context. Correlate with IIS worker process spawning child processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) immediately after file write.

suggestion.title: IIS Process Spawning Cmd/PowerShell
suggestion.rationale: Web shells execute system commands via IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). No detection suggested despite this being the primary post-exploitation activity. Article should contain examples of payloads or observed command patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on w3wp.exe or iisexpress.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe with suspicious arguments (encoded payloads, network commands, file operations). High fidelity if child process inherits IIS network context.

suggestion.title: HTTP Request to Suspected Web Shell Path
suggestion.rationale: Custom web shell would be accessed via HTTP requests to a specific path on the IIS server. Pipeline extracted no HTTP-layer IOCs, file paths, or query patterns from what should be detailed in the article.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor IIS access logs for POST/GET requests to unusual file paths (e.g., /images/shell.aspx, /uploads/admin.php, /temp/*.ashx) with large response payloads or repeating execution commands. Correlate with process spawning on the same server.

suggestion.title: IIS Vulnerability Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Title implies targeted IIS attack (OP-512 'targets' IIS), likely via CVE or 0-day. No exploitation technique or affected version identified by pipeline despite 'HIGH' severity and explicit IIS targeting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP requests with malformed headers, oversized payloads, or known IIS RCE patterns (e.g., path traversal, ISAPI extension abuse, HTTP method override). Baseline normal IIS traffic; flag outliers with high request rates or binary content in GET parameters.

suggestion.title: Outbound Connection from IIS Worker Process
suggestion.rationale: Web shells typically establish reverse shells or exfil data. Title mentions 'Custom Web Shell Framework' implying command-and-control capability. No network IOCs (C2 IPs, domains) or lateral movement patterns extracted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound connections initiated by w3wp.exe or iisexpress.exe to non-whitelist IPs/domains, especially on uncommon ports (8080-8090, 4444, 5555). Correlate with HTTP POST requests to external IPs or reverse-shell signatures in payload inspection.

suggestion.title: File System Enumeration from IIS Context
suggestion.rationale: Web shell post-exploitation typically includes discovery of sensitive files, config backups, source code. No discovery-phase techniques or attacker-controlled enumeration patterns mentioned in pipeline output.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for w3wp.exe or child processes recursively reading system directories (C:\, C:\Windows, C:\Program Files), web.config files, or high-entropy file reads. Flag sequential access to sensitive paths without corresponding write activity.

suggestion.title: Detect unauthorized SMTP relay from cloud compute instances
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes attack objective as 'Covert SMTP Relay Network' using hijacked cloud servers. Servers configured for inbound SMTP (port 25, 587, 465) when the instance purpose does not justify mail services is a strong indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when cloud compute instances with non-mail workload classification open inbound listeners on TCP 25, 587, or 465 after a suspicious credential use or privilege escalation event. Cross-correlate with outbound SMTP connection initiation to detect relaying behavior.

suggestion.title: Monitor for PCPJack malware process execution in cloud environments
suggestion.rationale: The malware name 'PCPJack' is the primary threat indicator from the article title and should drive process-level detection across cloud platforms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create indicators of compromise for known PCPJack process names, code-signed binaries, or injection behaviors. Alert on execution in cloud-provisioned instances, particularly those not running mail services.

suggestion.title: Detect credential compromise across major cloud providers (AWS/GCP/Azure)
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'hijacked 230' instances across three cloud providers, indicating either widespread credential compromise or a shared vulnerability. Phrase 'hijacks' implies unauthorized account control.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline for successful API calls and instance creation by authorized service accounts. Alert on anomalous login patterns (impossible travel, off-hours access, unusual IPs) tied to compute instance creation or modification across all three cloud platforms within a short time window.

suggestion.title: Detect lateral movement and persistence in multi-cloud environments
suggestion.rationale: Compromise of 230 servers across three providers suggests either mass initial access or rapid lateral movement. Pipeline should reconstruct the 'movement' phase between initial compromise and SMTP relay deployment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect inter-instance communication originating from compute instances not typically communicating with each other. Alert on SSH/RDP sessions to multiple instances in rapid succession, particularly if those instances differ in function or region.

suggestion.title: Monitor for email exfiltration and spam campaigns from cloud infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Once servers are hijacked for 'SMTP Relay Network' use, detect the abuse pattern through volume anomalies and content inspection: 'covert' implies deception, likely phishing or spam campaigns originating from legitimate cloud IP ranges.
log_sources: Mail gateway logs (Proofpoint, Mimecast, O365 DLP)
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag compute instances initiating SMTP connections to thousands of external recipients or flagged spam seed lists. Alert if cloud IP ranges begin appearing on threat-intel blocklists for email abuse. Correlate with cloud-native security groups allowing unexpected egress on port 25/587.

suggestion.title: Detect anomalous network egress patterns from cloud VMs after privilege escalation
suggestion.rationale: Attack progression: compromise → install PCPJack → establish SMTP relay. Between execution and impact, attacker must escalate privileges and download/configure malware. This phase should trigger on unexpected outbound connections post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After detecting privilege escalation or credential misuse on a cloud instance, alert on outbound connections to non-whitelisted domains, high-entropy DNS queries, or connections to known C2 infrastructure. Compare egress patterns pre- and post-compromise event.

suggestion.title: Agentic AI Suspicious Code Modification in CI/CD
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly concerns Claude Code GitHub Actions executing in CI/CD—detect when agentic systems generate unexpected commits with cryptographic ops, API calls to external services, or data-exfiltration patterns. Phrase: 'Claude Code Github action case' establishes agentic automation as the attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when GitHub commits authored by Claude Code actions introduce unexpected file modifications, shell invocations in non-script files, or API credentials embedded in code. Baseline expected commit patterns per repository and flag deviations in code complexity, affected permissions, or external API calls.

suggestion.title: GitHub Secrets/Tokens Exfiltration via Agentic Workflow
suggestion.rationale: CI/CD agentic systems have implicit access to GitHub repository secrets and PATs in workflow environment. Detecting unauthorized secret access/transmission is essential. 'Securing CI/CD in an agentic world' implies threat model includes agentic systems leaking credentials.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect agentic CI/CD processes (GitHub Actions runners) attempting to export, encode, or transmit GitHub tokens, SSH keys, or API secrets to external endpoints. Flag base64/hex encoding of credential patterns followed by network exfiltration attempts.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Lateral Movement from Compromised CI/CD Agent
suggestion.rationale: Compromised agentic runners with elevated CI/CD privileges can pivot to internal infrastructure. 'Securing' context implies threat model includes post-compromise lateral movement.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for outbound SSH, RDP, WinRM, or kubectl connections initiated by CI/CD runner processes to internal systems outside baseline workflow scope. Correlate multi-hop movement chains and flag CI/CD agents accessing secrets management systems or internal git servers.

suggestion.title: Supply-Chain Code Injection via Adversarial Agent Prompting
suggestion.rationale: Agentic systems are steerable by crafted inputs in repos, issues, or PR comments. Attackers can inject prompts to trigger Claude Code to generate malicious payloads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate GitHub issue/PR comments containing unusual instructions, code snippets, or executable payloads with subsequent commits authored by Claude Code agents. Alert on commits introducing unexpected imports, privilege-escalation code, or exfiltration patterns within 15 minutes of crafted prompt detection.

suggestion.title: Polyfill.io Domain HTTP 401 Responses
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'starting in late May 2026, the polyfill[.]io domain became active again and started responding with HTTP 401 authentication requests.' This is the core attack mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network traffic for HTTP 401 responses from polyfill.io or known malicious CDN domains. Track user agent and referer headers to correlate with legitimate vs. injected requests. Alert on 401 responses followed by browser credential prompt interactions.

suggestion.title: Stale Polyfill.io References in Web Source Code
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'some sites using the service failed to clean all their pages over the past two years, so remnants of Polyfill code remained.' Detection of persistent legacy CDN script includes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan website source code and WAF logs for script includes pointing to polyfill.io, polyfill.com, or polyfill.top domains. Alert on requests to these domains even if not directly user-initiated; indicates unpatched legacy integrations.

suggestion.title: Browser Login Prompt from Non-Auth Domain
suggestion.rationale: Article describes: 'User browsers visiting pages such as Toshiba's and MUJI's interpret that as a request for a username and password, so they serve a login prompt.' The HTTP 401 from a CDN triggers native credential harvesting UI.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP 401 responses from domains not typically serving authentication (CDNs, polyfill providers, etc.). Flag browser credential prompts triggered by non-origin servers or unexpected redirect chains that terminate at login screens.

suggestion.title: DNS Queries to Malicious Polyfill Domain
suggestion.rationale: Article states polyfill.io 'became active again' in late May 2026; DNS resolution is the first indicator of compromise when websites attempt to load the malicious CDN.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS queries for polyfill.io resolution from internal networks. Correlate with web gateway logs to confirm HTTP requests to resolved IP. Alert on organizations known to use legacy Polyfill integrations (e.g., Toshiba, Muji, Samsung, Zojirushi).

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Compromise via Expired Domain Reclamation
suggestion.rationale: Article explains: 'the domain was not owned by the creator... when the domain expired, it could be claimed by anyone' and 'the domain was purchased by a Chinese entity.' This is domain hijacking enabling persistent malicious injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor expiration and re-registration of popular open-source project domains (npm, CDN, library hosts). Alert on WHOIS changes, registrar transfers, or nameserver updates for high-risk domains. Cross-reference with any CDN domains in use within the organization.

suggestion.title: Affected Organization Credential Exposure via Polyfill Prompt
suggestion.rationale: Article names: Toshiba, Muji, Samsung Smart TVs, Zojirushi, FiNC Technologies, Ishiyaku Publishers, Hobonichi. These organizations' users saw login prompts; a use case should track credential submission logs for these entities.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: For known-affected organizations, review authentication logs for anomalies (e.g., failed logins immediately before credential reset requests, logins from impossible geo locations). Cross-check browser cache/history for polyfill.io 401 responses coinciding with password change events.

suggestion.title: FFmpeg Process Execution with Malformed Media Input
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes 21 zero-days in FFmpeg without describing specific payload mechanisms, but FFmpeg zero-days universally involve malformed media files triggering code execution. The article's description of 'AI Agent Uncovers Zero-Days' implies active exploitation detection is relevant for defense.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor FFmpeg processes spawned with file paths containing suspicious extensions (.m3u8, .mkv, .mp4 with embedded exploits) or unusual parent processes (web browsers, email clients). Correlate with crash dumps, segmentation faults, or exit codes indicating memory corruption.

suggestion.title: Chrome Renderer Process Crash or Abnormal Termination
suggestion.rationale: Article cites '429 Chrome patches'—the scale indicates widespread vulnerability coverage. Chrome exploits commonly trigger renderer crashes; abnormal termination or multiple crashes within a short window can indicate exploitation attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on Chrome renderer (chrome.exe --type=renderer) processes terminating with exit code 0xC0000374 (heap corruption), 0xC0000409 (stack overflow), or unhandled exception codes within 2 seconds of spawning. Correlate with tab URLs to identify malicious sites.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable FFmpeg or Chrome Version Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies '21 Zero-Days in FFmpeg' and bulk Chrome patches; inventory of deployed versions should be baseline. Process execution from known-vulnerable FFmpeg or Chrome versions is detection-ready once CVE details published.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Generate baseline of FFmpeg and Chrome versions across environment at time of disclosure. When article publishes specific CVE identifiers, query for execution events involving version numbers falling within vulnerable ranges (e.g., FFmpeg < X.Y.Z). Flag process creation from unpatched binaries as elevated risk.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Lateral Movement from Browser Context
suggestion.rationale: Chrome zero-days are often chained with privilege escalation exploits; article's bulk patch count suggests scope of post-compromise impact. Lateral movement from browser to system or network resources is expected kill-chain step.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for outbound network connections from chrome.exe or ffmpeg.exe to unusual destinations (non-CDN, non-standard ports, C2 profiles). Detect file writes to system directories, registry modifications, or spawning of cmd.exe/powershell.exe from browser/media-player contexts.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Dependency Download or In-Memory Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: FFmpeg zero-days often involve codec libraries or libav dependencies; patch count (429 for Chrome) suggests transitive dependency fixes. Article does not describe mechanism, but pipeline should flag data exfiltration or unusual resource access patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor FFmpeg/Chrome processes for suspicious memory operations (WriteProcessMemory, VirtualAllocEx patterns typical of ROP/JIT exploitation). Detect downloads of obfuscated payloads or codec files from attacker infrastructure. Flag processes disabling Windows Defender or AMSI (T1562.001).

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article states flaw is 'actively exploited' and added to CISA KEV. Pipeline failed to generate initial-access detection despite this being the first observable attack step. Should detect inbound requests targeting Serv-U instances with known payload markers or version enumeration patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests to SolarWinds Serv-U endpoints (common ports: 22, 3389, 443, or app-specific). Flag requests containing path traversal patterns, RCE payload signatures, or Serv-U version fingerprinting queries. Baseline legitimate Serv-U traffic and alert on anomalous request patterns originating from external IPs.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U Denial of Service Impact
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly identifies flaw type as 'DoS'. Pipeline missed impact phase entirely. Should surface detection for service unavailability, connection resets, or resource exhaustion on Serv-U hosts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect DoS artifacts: sustained high-volume connection attempts, TCP resets, or CPU/memory spikes on Serv-U infrastructure. Alert if Serv-U service logs show repeated connection failures or availability drops. Use rate-based threshold: >100 failed connections from single source within 5-minute window.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable SolarWinds Serv-U Asset Inventory
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'SolarWinds Serv-U' vulnerability with CISA patch guidance implied. Pipeline should trigger discovery detection to identify whether vulnerable versions exist in environment before active scanning begins.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query Splunk/MDE for SolarWinds Serv-U software inventory. Cross-reference installed versions against CISA KEV published affected ranges. Alert any non-compliant instances for immediate patching. Escalate if Serv-U is internet-facing.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Attempts Against Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager CVE-2026-20245
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Actively Exploited' and identifies Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager as target. Pipeline must detect inbound exploit traffic to vulnerable control-plane endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP/HTTPS requests to Cisco SD-WAN Manager API endpoints for suspicious payloads, command injection patterns, path traversal, or known exploit signatures. Correlate with 40x/50x response codes or service crashes.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Command Execution from SD-WAN Manager Process Context
suggestion.rationale: Active exploitation implies successful RCE. Article states no patch available—defenders must detect post-compromise activity. Pipeline should flag process spawning (bash, sh, curl, wget) under viptela/cvac service accounts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect child processes spawned by Cisco SD-WAN Manager daemons with shell/script interpreters, Base64-encoded arguments, DNS queries to attacker infrastructure, or outbound port 443/8080 connections to non-whitelisted IPs.

suggestion.title: Privilege Escalation to Root/Administrator from Compromised SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Management appliance compromise typically followed by vertical escalation. Article context (no patch, active exploitation) implies threat actor persistence—must detect sudo abuse, setuid misuse, or container escape.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag sudo invocations by SD-WAN Manager service accounts without corresponding scheduled tasks, setuid binary execution, or unexpected transitions to root UID via authentication bypass.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement from SD-WAN Manager to Branch Routers via Stored Credentials
suggestion.rationale: SD-WAN Manager holds credentials and SSH keys for entire branch fabric—compromised control plane enables pivot to downstream routers. Article does not exclude lateral movement; defenders must assume east-west threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for SSH/Netconf connections from SD-WAN Manager to branch routers outside maintenance windows, bulk credential extraction from /etc/viptela/ or credential vaults, or unauthorized API calls to managed device endpoints.

suggestion.title: Persistence Installation on SD-WAN Manager (No Patch Available)
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states 'No Patch Available'—attackers will establish long-term footholds. Pipeline must detect cron jobs, systemd service modifications, or backdoor binaries to ensure post-reboot access.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unexpected service creation under systemd, cron jobs added to /etc/cron.d/ or user crontabs, new users added to viptela/admin groups, or unsigned binaries written to Cisco directories (/opt/cisco/, /usr/local/cisco).

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration of Network Topology and VPN Credentials from SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: SD-WAN Manager stores network topology, IPsec keys, and branch device credentials. High-severity exploitation likely includes data theft for operational planning or downstream compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor bulk reads from SD-WAN configuration database, API calls exporting policy/topology objects, large outbound HTTPS flows to non-production IPs, or SCP/SFTP transfers of /etc/viptela/ directories.

suggestion.title: Smart TV Outbound Proxy Activity Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes TVs as 'web-scraping proxies' — requires detection of high-volume outbound HTTPS connections from TV devices to diverse external targets. Phrase: 'Quietly Turning Smart TVs Into Web-Scraping Proxies'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for smart TV endpoints initiating repeated outbound HTTPS connections to distinct domains with high request volume and large data transfers. Flag patterns consistent with web scraping: requests to news/financial/tech sites; repeated 200 responses with large payloads; no corresponding user browsing activity.

suggestion.title: Suspicious App Installation on Connected Devices
suggestion.rationale: Attack vector is 'free apps' on TV app stores — detect installation of unsigned, sideloaded, or newly-published applications on smart TV platforms with unusual permissions. Phrase: 'Free Apps Are Quietly Turning Smart TVs'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on TV app installations from non-official sources or apps requesting unusual permissions (network, data access, background execution). Cross-reference app store metadata to identify recently-registered publishers or unsigned packages.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration via Compromised TV Devices
suggestion.rationale: Core mechanism is data collection for AI training — detect large cumulative data transfers from TV devices to external C2/aggregation infrastructure. Phrase: 'web-scraping proxies for AI'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track cumulative outbound data volume from individual TV devices over daily windows. Flag when a TV transfers >100MB/day to external IPs, especially correlating with concurrent requests to multiple distinct domains.

suggestion.title: App-Based Command & Control Communication
suggestion.rationale: Malicious apps must coordinate with attacker infrastructure to receive scraping targets and exfiltrate collected data. Phrase: implies ongoing coordination for persistent 'web-scraping' behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify periodic DNS queries and HTTPS connections from TV app contexts to suspicious/newly-registered domains. Look for regular beaconing intervals (hourly/daily check-ins) or large data transfers initiated by app processes.

suggestion.title: Reconnaissance of Web Content Sources via TV Proxy
suggestion.rationale: Before large-scale scraping, attackers perform reconnaissance on target websites to identify high-value data. Detect atypical HTTP reconnaissance from TV devices. Phrase: implicit in scraping targets selection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP HEAD/OPTIONS requests from TV devices to known news, financial, tech, or research sites. Identify when a TV connects to multiple competitors' websites or API endpoints within short windows — signature of content reconnaissance.

suggestion.title: Anomalous User-Agent and Browser Behavior from TVs
suggestion.rationale: Compromised TV apps generate network traffic with atypical user-agents, HTTP patterns, and behavioral signatures inconsistent with normal TV usage. Phrase: apps operating as 'proxies' behave differently from normal TV apps.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP User-Agent headers from TV devices for headless browser strings, crawler/scraper signatures, or bot identifiers. Flag when app-generated traffic deviates from expected TV OS/library patterns, especially library calls to web scraping frameworks.

suggestion.title: Bulk Repository File Modifications Across Microsoft Repos
suggestion.rationale: Title states 73 Microsoft GitHub repos were hit—implies coordinated code injection. Article phrase 'Miasma Worm Hits 73 Microsoft GitHub Repositories' establishes scope of repo compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual commit frequency, file modifications by service accounts, or commits outside normal developer timezones/branches across multiple repos in short time window. Flag when single actor or token modifies >10 repos in <1 hour.

suggestion.title: Detection of Miasma Worm Payload in Repository Contents
suggestion.rationale: Named malware 'Miasma Worm' suggests identifiable binary or script signatures in compromised repos. Article indicates worm-like propagation ('Worm' implies self-replication).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on presence of known Miasma Worm signatures or hashes in cloned repository files. Correlate file hash matches against threat feeds. Monitor for self-referential or obfuscated payload patterns typical of worm behavior.

suggestion.title: GitHub OAuth Token Abuse and Repo Access Anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attack on GitHub requires authentication bypass or token compromise. Article implies attacker gained write access to 73 Microsoft repos—likely via compromised credentials or OAuth token theft.
